1. Fungible Token dApp (templates/token-dapp/)

Overview

A full-stack starter kit for creating, distributing, and managing SEP-41 compliant fungible tokens.

Key Capabilities

  • Smart Contract: SEP-41 token operations (transfer, transfer_from, approve, mint, burn, balance, allowance, decimals, name, symbol).
  • Storage Strategy: Instance storage for global metadata and persistent storage with automated TTL extension for user balances.
  • Frontend Dashboard: Live balance query, token transfer form, admin mint modal, and Freighter wallet integration.

Quick Start

cd templates/token-dapp/contracts/token
cargo test

2. NFT Marketplace dApp (templates/nft-marketplace-dapp/)

Overview

A full-stack digital collectible and marketplace dApp for minting NFTs and trading them at fixed prices.

Key Capabilities

  • Smart Contract: On-chain NFT minting with URI metadata, fixed-price listing, contract escrow, atomic payment settlement, and listing cancellation.
  • Security: Verified seller ownership, state mutation atomicity, and safe delisting.
  • Frontend Gallery: Visual collectible grid, minting modal, listing cards with price in XLM, and 1-click buy button.

Quick Start

The NFT marketplace template is a single package that is a member of the cookbook Cargo workspace, so it is built and tested with the workspace soroban-sdk. From the repository root:

cargo test -p nft-marketplace-dapp

Or from inside the template directory:

cd templates/nft-marketplace-dapp
cargo test

3. DAO Governance & Treasury dApp (templates/dao-governance-dapp/)

Overview

A full-stack community governance portal for managing proposals, voting with token weights, and executing treasury disbursements.

Key Capabilities

  • Smart Contract: Proposal registration, weighted voting, quorum and threshold validation, and execution timelocks.
  • Security: Single-vote per account enforcement, ledger sequence time checks, and status validation.
  • Frontend Portal: Active proposal dashboard, live vote tally bars (For/Against), proposal submission modal, and execution trigger.

Quick Start

cd templates/dao-governance-dapp/contracts/governance
cargo test

Common Architecture & Best Practices

All templates implement the following architectural guarantees:

  1. Explicit Authorization: Critical state mutations require from.require_auth() or admin.require_auth().
  2. Checked Arithmetic: Zero integer overflow or underflow risks using Rust’s checked arithmetic.
  3. Storage TTL Management: Both instance and persistent entries have their TTL refreshed to prevent unexpected state archival.
  4. Auditable Events: Standard topics emitted for off-chain indexing.
  5. No Placeholders: Fully functional contracts, complete unit tests, and interactive demo UIs.

Playground Infrastructure

The Soroban Cookbook playground is the local Cargo workspace at the root of this repository. There is no separate service to install — cloning the repo gives you a working playground for every example in the book.

Framework

The playground is a standard Rust/Cargo workspace (see the root Cargo.toml). Every example lives under examples/ as its own workspace member, so you can build, edit, and test any single example without touching the others.

Soroban SDK Integration

The soroban-sdk version is pinned once, at the workspace level:

[workspace.dependencies]
soroban-sdk = "26.0.0-rc.1"

Each example crate depends on soroban-sdk.workspace = true, so every contract in the playground builds against the same SDK version.

Build System

# Add the Wasm target once
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown

# Build a single example
cargo build --manifest-path examples/basics/01-hello-world/Cargo.toml \
            --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release

# Build every workspace member
cargo build --workspace --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release

Testing Capability

# Test a single example
cargo test --manifest-path examples/basics/01-hello-world/Cargo.toml

# Test the full workspace
cargo test --workspace

Cross-example integration and security tests live in tests/integration and tests/security, and are included as workspace members so cargo test --workspace runs them alongside the individual examples.

Use-Case Examples

Beyond the basics, the playground ships complete use-case contracts grouped by domain. Each category is a set of workspace members under examples/, so you can build, test, and experiment with any of them directly.

DeFi (examples/defi/)

Lending, liquidity, and market primitives — e.g. a token swap pool, a simple lending market, and a staking rewards contract.

cargo test --workspace --manifest-path examples/defi/Cargo.toml

NFTs (examples/nfts/)

NFT minting, metadata, and marketplace flows — e.g. a collectible with royalties and a fixed-price marketplace.

cargo test --workspace --manifest-path examples/nfts/Cargo.toml

Governance (examples/governance/)

On-chain decision making — e.g. proposal creation, token-weighted voting, and timelocked execution.

cargo test --workspace --manifest-path examples/governance/Cargo.toml

Tokens (examples/tokens/)

Fungible token patterns — e.g. a standard token, a wrapped asset, and a vesting token.

cargo test --workspace --manifest-path examples/tokens/Cargo.toml

To build every use-case example at once:

cargo build --workspace --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release

Documentation

  • Interactive Playground — Basic Examples walks through all 14 basics examples with runnable snippets.
  • Setup Environment covers installing Rust, the Wasm target, and the Soroban CLI from scratch.
  • Testing Guide covers mocking auth, time manipulation, and event assertions when writing your own tests.

1. Token Examples

1.1 SEP-41 token — the base layer

Example: examples/tokens/01-sep41-token Book page: Token Examples →

A fungible token implements the SEP-41 interface: balance, transfer, allowance, approve, transfer_from, burn and burn_from.

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]

fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env};

#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum DataKey {
    Balance(Address),
    Allowance(Address, Address),
}

#[contract]
pub struct TokenContract;

#[contractimpl]
impl TokenContract {
    /// Moves `amount` from `from` to `to`.
    pub fn transfer(env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128) {
        // The owner of the funds must sign for the transfer.
        from.require_auth();

        let mut from_balance: i128 = env
            .storage()
            .persistent()
            .get(&DataKey::Balance(from.clone()))
            .unwrap_or(0);
        let to_balance: i128 = env
            .storage()
            .persistent()
            .get(&DataKey::Balance(to.clone()))
            .unwrap_or(0);

        from_balance -= amount;
        let to_balance = to_balance.checked_add(amount).unwrap();

        env.storage()
            .persistent()
            .set(&DataKey::Balance(from), &from_balance);
        env.storage()
            .persistent()
            .set(&DataKey::Balance(to), &to_balance);
    }

    pub fn balance(env: Env, user: Address) -> i128 {
        env.storage()
            .persistent()
            .get(&DataKey::Balance(user))
            .unwrap_or(0)
    }
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/tokens/01-sep41-token
cargo test

What to edit: remove from.require_auth() and re-run the tests — the contract no longer enforces ownership of the funds.

1.2 Allowance pattern — “spending” someone else’s balance

Example: examples/tokens/05-allowance-pattern Book page: Token Examples →

An allowance lets a spender move funds on behalf of an owner, with an expiry ledger so stale approvals die automatically.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// The owner approves `spender` to move up to `amount`.
pub fn approve(
    env: Env,
    owner: Address,
    spender: Address,
    amount: i128,
    expiration_ledger: u32,
) -> Result<(), AllowanceError> {
    owner.require_auth();
    if amount < 0 {
        return Err(AllowanceError::InvalidAmount);
    }
    if expiration_ledger < env.ledger().sequence() {
        return Err(AllowanceError::InvalidExpiration);
    }
    env.storage().persistent().set(
        &DataKey::Allowance(owner, spender),
        &AllowanceValue { amount, expiration_ledger },
    );
    Ok(())
}

/// The spender moves `amount` out of the owner's balance.
pub fn transfer_from(
    env: Env,
    spender: Address,
    owner: Address,
    to: Address,
    amount: i128,
) -> Result<(), AllowanceError> {
    spender.require_auth();

    let allowance = read_allowance(&env, &owner, &spender);
    // An expired allowance is worth nothing.
    if allowance.amount == 0
        || (allowance.expiration_ledger < env.ledger().sequence())
    {
        return Err(AllowanceError::InsufficientAllowance);
    }
    if allowance.amount < amount {
        return Err(AllowanceError::InsufficientAllowance);
    }
    // ... move the funds and decrement the allowance
    Ok(())
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/tokens/05-allowance-pattern
cargo test

What to edit: drop the expiry check in read_allowance and see the “expired allowance” integration test fail — approvals must expire.

1.3 Token wrapper — composing two tokens

Example: examples/tokens/06-token-wrapper Book page: Token Examples →

A wrapper contract holds an underlying token and exposes it under a new address — the classic building block for vault shares and receipt tokens.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// Wrap `amount` of the underlying token into wrapper shares.
pub fn deposit(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<i128, TokenWrapperError> {
    user.require_auth();

    // Pull the underlying tokens into this contract first ...
    self::TokenClient::new(&env, &underlying).transfer(
        &user,
        &env.current_contract_address(),
        &amount,
    );

    // ... then credit the wrapper shares.
    let shares = deposit_internal(&env, &user, amount);
    Ok(shares)
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/tokens/06-token-wrapper
cargo test

2. Cross-Contract Examples

2.1 Ajo factory — deploying contracts from a contract

Example: examples/intermediate/ajo-factory Book page: Ajo Factory →

A factory stores a Wasm hash and derives a unique address per deployment, so every instance is isolated but reproducible.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// Deploy a new instance of the template contract.
pub fn deploy(env: Env, salt: BytesN<32>) -> Result<Address, FactoryError> {
    let wasm_hash: BytesN<32> = env
        .storage()
        .instance()
        .get(&DataKey::TemplateWasm)
        .ok_or(FactoryError::NotInitialized)?;

    // `with_current_contract` derives a deterministic address from the salt.
    let address = env
        .deployer()
        .with_current_contract(salt)
        .deploy(wasm_hash);

    env.storage()
        .instance()
        .set(&DataKey::DeployedAjo(address.clone()), &true);
    Ok(address)
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/intermediate/ajo-factory
cargo test

2.2 Contract registry — one address to rule them all

Example: examples/advanced/contract-registry Book page: Advanced Examples →

A registry maps a human-friendly name to a contract address and lets callers reach other contracts through a single entry point.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// Register `implementation` under `name`.
pub fn register(env: Env, name: Symbol, implementation: Address) -> Result<(), RegistryError> {
    admin(&env)?.require_auth();
    env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Contract(name), &implementation);
    Ok(())
}

/// Forward a call to the contract registered under `name`.
pub fn call(env: Env, name: Symbol, fn_name: Symbol, args: Vec<Val>) -> Result<Val, RegistryError> {
    let target: Address = env
        .storage()
        .persistent()
        .get(&DataKey::Contract(name))
        .ok_or(RegistryError::NotFound)?;
    Ok(env.invoke_contract::<Val>(&target, &fn_name, args))
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/advanced/contract-registry
cargo test

2.3 Oracle pattern — reading external data

Example: examples/advanced/03-oracle-pattern Book page: Oracle Pattern →

Contracts cannot fetch prices on their own; an oracle contract is updated by privileged sources and read by everyone else.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// Publish a new price.  Only trusted oracles may do this.
pub fn update_price(env: Env, oracle: Address, asset: Symbol, price: i128) -> Result<(), OracleError> {
    if !env.storage().persistent().has(&DataKey::Oracle(oracle.clone())) {
        return Err(OracleError::Unauthorized);
    }
    oracle.require_auth();
    env.storage()
        .persistent()
        .set(&DataKey::Price(asset.clone(), price), &price);
    Ok(())
}

/// Read the last published price.
pub fn get_price(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Result<i128, OracleError> {
    env.storage()
        .persistent()
        .get(&DataKey::Price(asset))
        .ok_or(OracleError::NotFound)
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/advanced/03-oracle-pattern
cargo test

3. Access Control Examples

3.1 Role-based access control

Example: examples/intermediate/02-role-based-access-control Book page: Intermediate Examples →

Roles are stored per address. Every guarded function checks the role of the caller before it touches state.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
#[repr(u32)]
pub enum Role {
    Admin = 0,
    Moderator = 1,
    User = 2,
}

#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum DataKey {
    Role(Address, Role),
    Admin,
}

/// True when `account` holds `role`.
pub fn has_role(env: &Env, account: &Address, role: Role) -> bool {
    env.storage().persistent().has(&DataKey::Role(account.clone(), role))
}

/// Guard used by the privileged entry points.
fn require_role(env: &Env, account: &Address, role: Role) {
    assert!(has_role(env, account, role), "unauthorized");
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/intermediate/02-role-based-access-control
cargo test

3.2 Hierarchical access control — roles that inherit

Example: examples/advanced/16-hierarchical-access-control Book page: Advanced Examples →

ADMIN > MANAGER > OPERATOR: a higher role inherits the permissions of all lower roles, so an admin never has to be granted permissions one by one.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub const ROLE_ADMIN: Symbol = symbol_short!("ADMIN");
pub const ROLE_MANAGER: Symbol = symbol_short!("MANAGER");
pub const ROLE_OPERATOR: Symbol = symbol_short!("OPERATOR");
pub const PERM_MANAGE_ROLES: Symbol = symbol_short!("MNG_ROLES");
pub const PERM_USE_RESOURCES: Symbol = symbol_short!("USE_RES");

/// Grant `role` to `account`.  Only callers that may manage `role` succeed.
pub fn grant_role(env: Env, caller: Address, role: Symbol, account: Address) {
    caller.require_auth();
    require_permission(&env, &caller, PERM_MANAGE_ROLES);
    assert!(can_manage_role(&env, &caller, &role), "Caller cannot manage target role");
    env.storage()
        .persistent()
        .set(&DataKey::RoleMembers(role), &account);
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/advanced/16-hierarchical-access-control
cargo test

3.3 Pause / unpause — the emergency brake

Example: examples/intermediate/03-pause-unpause Book page: Pause / Unpause →

A single flag halts every state-changing entry point while reads keep working.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// Reject the call when the contract is paused.
fn require_not_paused(env: &Env) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
    let paused: bool = env
        .storage()
        .instance()
        .get(&DataKey::Paused)
        .unwrap_or(false);
    if paused {
        Err(ContractError::ContractPaused)
    } else {
        Ok(())
    }
}

/// Emergency switch used by the admin.
pub fn pause(env: Env, admin: Address) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
    read_admin(&env)?.require_auth();
    env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Paused, &true);
    Ok(())
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/intermediate/03-pause-unpause
cargo test

Playground Tutorial 1: Your First Smart Contract

Overview

This step-by-step tutorial will guide you through creating and deploying your first Soroban smart contract using the interactive playground.

Duration: 15-20 minutes Difficulty: Beginner Prerequisites: Basic understanding of Rust syntax

Learning Objectives

  • Set up a contract in the playground
  • Write a simple “Hello World” contract
  • Deploy to a local network
  • Interact with the deployed contract

Step 1: Access the Playground

  1. Navigate to the Soroban Cookbook Playground
  2. You should see the editor interface with a default contract template
  3. Take a moment to explore the interface:
    • Editor panel (left): Write your Rust code
    • Terminal (bottom): Build and deploy commands
    • Contract status (right): Deployment information

Step 2: Write Your First Contract

Replace the template code with this simple hello world contract:

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Symbol, String as SorobanString};

#[contract]
pub struct HelloContract;

#[contractimpl]
impl HelloContract {
    pub fn hello(name: SorobanString) -> SorobanString {
        SorobanString::from_slice(&format!("Hello, {}!", name.clone()).as_str())
    }
    
    pub fn get_message() -> SorobanString {
        SorobanString::from_slice("Welcome to Soroban!")
    }
}
}

Step 3: Build Your Contract

  1. In the terminal, run:

    cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release

  2. Watch for the build output. You should see:

    • Compilation messages
    • Success confirmation: “Finished release”

  3. If there are errors, check:

    • Rust syntax correctness
    • Soroban SDK imports
    • Function signatures

Step 4: Deploy to Local Network

  1. Run the deployment command:

    soroban contract deploy --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/hello_world.wasm

  2. The terminal will output:

    • Network connection status
    • Contract deployment details
    • Contract ID (save this!)

  3. Copy the contract ID for the next step

Step 5: Interact with Your Contract

  1. Once deployed, use the contract client:

    soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn hello --arg "World"

  2. Expected output: "Hello, World!"

  3. Try the other function:

    soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn get_message

Step 6: Validation

Your contract successfully works if:

  • ✅ Build completes without errors
  • ✅ Deployment shows a contract ID
  • ✅ hello function returns the correct greeting
  • ✅ get_message function returns the welcome message

Common Issues & Solutions

Issue: Build fails with “cannot find crate”

  • Solution: Check that soroban-sdk is in your Cargo.toml

Issue: Deployment timeout

  • Solution: Verify network connection, restart the playground

Issue: Contract invoke returns undefined error

  • Solution: Ensure you’re using the correct contract ID and function name

Next Steps

  • Try modifying the contract to accept multiple parameters
  • Explore contract storage capabilities in Tutorial 2
  • Learn about contract errors in Tutorial 3

Tips & Hints

  • Always save your contract code before building
  • Use descriptive names for your functions
  • Test each function after deployment
  • Keep your contract ID safe for future interactions

Resources

  • Soroban SDK Documentation
  • Soroban Examples
  • Testing Guide

Summary

You’ve successfully:

  1. Written a Soroban smart contract
  2. Compiled it to WebAssembly
  3. Deployed it to a local network
  4. Invoked contract functions

Congratulations! You’re now ready to explore more advanced features.

Playground Tutorial 2: Working with Contract Storage

Overview

Learn how to persist data in your Soroban contracts using the storage layer. This tutorial covers storing and retrieving values.

Duration: 20-25 minutes Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate Prerequisites: Tutorial 1 completion

Learning Objectives

  • Understand contract storage mechanics
  • Implement persistent state
  • Read and write storage values
  • Handle storage errors

Step 1: Understanding Storage

Soroban contracts have access to:

  • Persistent Storage: Long-term data storage on the ledger
  • Temporary Storage: Short-lived data
  • Instance Storage: Contract-instance specific data

Step 2: Create a Counter Contract

Replace your previous contract with this storage-enabled example:

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, symbol_short, Symbol, Env};

#[contract]
pub struct CounterContract;

const COUNTER: Symbol = symbol_short!("count");

#[contractimpl]
impl CounterContract {
    /// Initialize the counter with a starting value
    pub fn init(env: Env, initial_value: u32) -> u32 {
        env.storage().instance().set(&COUNTER, &initial_value);
        initial_value
    }
    
    /// Increment the counter by 1
    pub fn increment(env: Env) -> u32 {
        let current: u32 = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&COUNTER)
            .unwrap_or(Ok(0u32))
            .unwrap_or(0u32);
        
        let new_value = current + 1;
        env.storage().instance().set(&COUNTER, &new_value);
        new_value
    }
    
    /// Get the current counter value
    pub fn get_count(env: Env) -> u32 {
        env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&COUNTER)
            .unwrap_or(Ok(0u32))
            .unwrap_or(0u32)
    }
    
    /// Reset the counter to zero
    pub fn reset(env: Env) {
        env.storage().instance().set(&COUNTER, &0u32);
    }
}
}

Step 3: Build and Deploy

  1. Build the contract:

    cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release

  2. Deploy:

    soroban contract deploy --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/counter_contract.wasm

  3. Save the contract ID

Step 4: Initialize the Counter

Initialize with starting value of 10:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn init --arg 10

Expected output: 10

Step 5: Test Storage Operations

Get the current value:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn get_count

Expected: 10

Increment the counter:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn increment

Expected: 11

Verify the increment persisted:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn get_count

Expected: 11 (not 10!)

Increment again:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn increment

Expected: 12

Reset the counter:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn reset

Verify the reset:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn get_count

Expected: 0

Step 6: Validation Checklist

✅ Contract builds successfully ✅ Contract deploys without errors ✅ init sets the starting value ✅ get_count returns the current value ✅ increment increases the value by 1 ✅ Values persist between contract calls ✅ reset sets the counter to 0

Storage Best Practices

  1. Use short symbols for storage keys to minimize gas costs
  2. Handle missing keys gracefully - use .unwrap_or() or similar
  3. Type your storage values - use consistent types
  4. Document storage layout in your contract comments
  5. Consider storage costs when designing data structures

Common Patterns

Pattern 1: Safe Value Retrieval

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let value = env.storage()
    .instance()
    .get(&KEY)
    .unwrap_or(Ok(0u32))
    .unwrap_or(0u32);
}

Pattern 2: Conditional Update

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let mut current = get_stored_value(&env);
if should_update {
    current += 1;
    env.storage().instance().set(&KEY, &current);
}
}

Pattern 3: Multiple Key Storage

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
const KEY_A: Symbol = symbol_short!("key_a");
const KEY_B: Symbol = symbol_short!("key_b");

env.storage().instance().set(&KEY_A, &value_a);
env.storage().instance().set(&KEY_B, &value_b);
}

Troubleshooting

Issue: “Value not found” error

  • Solution: Check that you’ve initialized the key first

Issue: Type mismatch errors

  • Solution: Ensure storage key types match when reading/writing

Issue: Storage operations are expensive

  • Solution: Batch multiple operations in a single transaction

Advanced Topics to Explore

  • Persistent storage vs. instance storage
  • Storage cost optimization
  • Complex data structures
  • Storage migration patterns

Next Steps

  • Tutorial 3: Error Handling and Validation
  • Tutorial 4: Authentication and Authorization
  • Tutorial 5: Multi-Contract Interactions

Summary

You’ve learned to:

  1. Use persistent storage in contracts
  2. Initialize and retrieve stored values
  3. Implement basic state management
  4. Handle storage operations safely

This foundation is crucial for building stateful smart contracts.

Playground Tutorial 3: Error Handling & Validation

Overview

Master error handling in Soroban contracts. Learn to validate inputs, define custom errors, and implement robust error handling patterns.

Duration: 25-30 minutes Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Tutorials 1-2 completion

Learning Objectives

  • Define custom contract errors
  • Implement input validation
  • Use Result types effectively
  • Provide helpful error messages

Step 1: Understanding Soroban Errors

Soroban errors are represented with custom error enums:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
#[repr(u32)]
pub enum ContractError {
    InvalidAmount = 1,
    Unauthorized = 2,
    AlreadyInitialized = 3,
    NotFound = 4,
}
}

Step 2: Create a Validated Wallet Contract

Build a contract with comprehensive error handling:

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{
    contract, contractimpl, symbol_short, Symbol, Env, Address,
};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
#[repr(u32)]
pub enum ContractError {
    InvalidAmount = 1,
    Unauthorized = 2,
    AlreadyInitialized = 3,
    InsufficientBalance = 4,
    MaxBalanceExceeded = 5,
}

impl Into<u32> for ContractError {
    fn into(self) -> u32 {
        self as u32
    }
}

#[contract]
pub struct WalletContract;

const OWNER: Symbol = symbol_short!("owner");
const BALANCE: Symbol = symbol_short!("bal");
const MAX_BALANCE: u128 = 1_000_000_000_000;

#[contractimpl]
impl WalletContract {
    /// Initialize wallet with owner
    pub fn init(env: Env, owner: Address) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
        // Check if already initialized
        if env.storage()
            .instance()
            .has(&OWNER)
        {
            return Err(ContractError::AlreadyInitialized);
        }
        
        env.storage().instance().set(&OWNER, &owner);
        env.storage().instance().set(&BALANCE, &0u128);
        Ok(())
    }
    
    /// Deposit funds
    pub fn deposit(
        env: Env,
        amount: u128,
    ) -> Result<u128, ContractError> {
        // Validate amount
        if amount == 0 {
            return Err(ContractError::InvalidAmount);
        }
        
        // Get current balance
        let current: u128 = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&BALANCE)
            .unwrap_or(Ok(0u128))
            .unwrap_or(0u128);
        
        // Check max balance
        let new_balance = current.checked_add(amount)
            .ok_or(ContractError::MaxBalanceExceeded)?;
        
        if new_balance > MAX_BALANCE {
            return Err(ContractError::MaxBalanceExceeded);
        }
        
        env.storage().instance().set(&BALANCE, &new_balance);
        Ok(new_balance)
    }
    
    /// Withdraw funds
    pub fn withdraw(
        env: Env,
        caller: Address,
        amount: u128,
    ) -> Result<u128, ContractError> {
        // Validate caller is owner
        let owner: Address = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&OWNER)
            .unwrap()
            .unwrap();
        
        if caller != owner {
            return Err(ContractError::Unauthorized);
        }
        
        // Validate amount
        if amount == 0 {
            return Err(ContractError::InvalidAmount);
        }
        
        // Get current balance
        let current: u128 = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&BALANCE)
            .unwrap_or(Ok(0u128))
            .unwrap_or(0u128);
        
        // Check sufficient balance
        if current < amount {
            return Err(ContractError::InsufficientBalance);
        }
        
        let new_balance = current - amount;
        env.storage().instance().set(&BALANCE, &new_balance);
        Ok(new_balance)
    }
    
    /// Get current balance
    pub fn get_balance(env: Env) -> u128 {
        env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&BALANCE)
            .unwrap_or(Ok(0u128))
            .unwrap_or(0u128)
    }
}
}

Step 3: Build and Deploy

  1. Build the contract:

    cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release

  2. Deploy:

    soroban contract deploy --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/wallet_contract.wasm

Step 4: Test Error Scenarios

Success Path - Valid Operations

Initialize wallet:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn init --arg <OWNER_ADDRESS>

Deposit 500:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn deposit --arg 500

Expected: 500

Check balance:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn get_balance

Expected: 500

Error Path - Invalid Operations

Try deposit with 0 amount:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn deposit --arg 0

Expected error: InvalidAmount (1)

Try initialize again:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn init --arg <OWNER_ADDRESS>

Expected error: AlreadyInitialized (3)

Try withdraw from non-owner account:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn withdraw --arg <DIFFERENT_OWNER> --arg 100

Expected error: Unauthorized (2)

Try withdraw more than balance:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn withdraw --arg <OWNER> --arg 1000

Expected error: InsufficientBalance (4)

Step 5: Validation Checklist

✅ Contract initializes successfully ✅ Valid deposits increase balance ✅ Invalid amounts are rejected with errors ✅ Unauthorized access is prevented ✅ Insufficient balance is detected ✅ Re-initialization is prevented ✅ Error codes are consistent

Error Handling Best Practices

  1. Be Specific: Define granular error types
  2. Validate Early: Check inputs at function entry
  3. Use Result Types: Return Result<T, E> for fallible operations
  4. Provide Context: Error messages should explain what went wrong
  5. Test Error Paths: Include error scenarios in tests

Common Patterns

Pattern 1: Checked Arithmetic

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let result = amount.checked_add(current)
    .ok_or(ContractError::Overflow)?;
}

Pattern 2: Authorization Check

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
if caller != expected_owner {
    return Err(ContractError::Unauthorized);
}
}

Pattern 3: State Validation

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
if env.storage().instance().has(&KEY) {
    return Err(ContractError::AlreadyInitialized);
}
}

Troubleshooting

Issue: Error codes not displaying correctly

  • Solution: Ensure #[repr(u32)] is on your error enum

Issue: Validation not working as expected

  • Solution: Check condition logic and operator precedence

Issue: Authorization always fails

  • Solution: Verify address equality comparison

Advanced Topics

  • Custom error context with structured data
  • Error recovery strategies
  • Graceful degradation patterns
  • Error logging and diagnostics

Next Steps

  • Tutorial 4: Authentication & Authorization
  • Tutorial 5: Multi-Contract Interactions
  • Explore Error Handling Examples

Summary

You now understand:

  1. How to define custom contract errors
  2. Implementing comprehensive input validation
  3. Using Rust Result types for error handling
  4. Testing both success and error paths
  5. Best practices for robust contracts

Error handling is critical for security and reliability!

Playground Tutorial 4: Authentication & Authorization

Overview

Learn to secure your Soroban contracts with authentication and authorization mechanisms. Control who can call what functions.

Duration: 30-35 minutes Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Tutorials 1-3 completion

Learning Objectives

  • Implement address-based authentication
  • Create role-based access control
  • Use the require_auth pattern
  • Verify caller identity

Step 1: Understanding Authentication vs Authorization

Authentication: Who are you?

  • Verify the caller’s identity
  • Use the require_auth() function

Authorization: What can you do?

  • Check caller’s permissions/roles
  • Compare against stored access rights

Step 2: Create a Bank Contract with Authorization

Build a contract with multi-user support:

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{
    contract, contractimpl, symbol_short, Symbol, Env, Address,
};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
#[repr(u32)]
pub enum ContractError {
    Unauthorized = 1,
    AlreadyInitialized = 2,
    InvalidAmount = 3,
    InsufficientBalance = 4,
    UserNotFound = 5,
}

impl Into<u32> for ContractError {
    fn into(self) -> u32 {
        self as u32
    }
}

#[contract]
pub struct BankContract;

const ADMIN: Symbol = symbol_short!("admin");
const BALANCE_PREFIX: &[u8] = b"bal_";

#[contractimpl]
impl BankContract {
    /// Initialize bank with admin
    pub fn init(env: Env, admin: Address) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
        if env.storage().instance().has(&ADMIN) {
            return Err(ContractError::AlreadyInitialized);
        }
        
        env.storage().instance().set(&ADMIN, &admin);
        Ok(())
    }
    
    /// Deposit funds to account
    pub fn deposit(
        env: Env,
        account: Address,
        amount: u128,
    ) -> Result<u128, ContractError> {
        // Verify caller is the account owner
        account.require_auth();
        
        // Validate amount
        if amount == 0 {
            return Err(ContractError::InvalidAmount);
        }
        
        // Get storage key for account
        let balance_key = get_balance_key(&account);
        
        // Get current balance
        let current: u128 = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&balance_key)
            .unwrap_or(Ok(0u128))
            .unwrap_or(0u128);
        
        let new_balance = current
            .checked_add(amount)
            .ok_or(ContractError::InvalidAmount)?;
        
        // Store new balance
        env.storage().instance().set(&balance_key, &new_balance);
        Ok(new_balance)
    }
    
    /// Withdraw funds from account
    pub fn withdraw(
        env: Env,
        account: Address,
        amount: u128,
    ) -> Result<u128, ContractError> {
        // Verify caller is the account owner
        account.require_auth();
        
        // Validate amount
        if amount == 0 {
            return Err(ContractError::InvalidAmount);
        }
        
        // Get storage key
        let balance_key = get_balance_key(&account);
        
        // Get current balance
        let current: u128 = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&balance_key)
            .unwrap_or(Ok(0u128))
            .unwrap_or(0u128);
        
        // Check sufficient balance
        if current < amount {
            return Err(ContractError::InsufficientBalance);
        }
        
        let new_balance = current - amount;
        env.storage().instance().set(&balance_key, &new_balance);
        Ok(new_balance)
    }
    
    /// Transfer funds between accounts
    pub fn transfer(
        env: Env,
        from: Address,
        to: Address,
        amount: u128,
    ) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
        // Verify caller is the sender
        from.require_auth();
        
        // Withdraw from sender
        self.withdraw(env.clone(), from.clone(), amount)?;
        
        // Deposit to recipient
        self.deposit(env, to, amount)?;
        
        Ok(())
    }
    
    /// Get account balance
    pub fn get_balance(env: Env, account: Address) -> u128 {
        let balance_key = get_balance_key(&account);
        env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&balance_key)
            .unwrap_or(Ok(0u128))
            .unwrap_or(0u128)
    }
    
    /// Admin-only function: reset account balance
    pub fn admin_reset_balance(
        env: Env,
        admin: Address,
        account: Address,
    ) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
        // Verify caller is admin
        admin.require_auth();
        
        // Check if caller is the actual admin
        let stored_admin: Address = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&ADMIN)
            .ok_or(ContractError::Unauthorized)?
            .map_err(|_| ContractError::Unauthorized)?;
        
        if admin != stored_admin {
            return Err(ContractError::Unauthorized);
        }
        
        // Reset balance
        let balance_key = get_balance_key(&account);
        env.storage().instance().set(&balance_key, &0u128);
        
        Ok(())
    }
}

/// Helper function to create balance storage key
fn get_balance_key(account: &Address) -> Symbol {
    // In production, use proper serialization
    symbol_short!("bal")
}
}

Step 3: Build and Deploy

  1. Build the contract:

    cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release

  2. Deploy:

    soroban contract deploy --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/bank_contract.wasm

Step 4: Test Authentication Flow

Setup Phase

Initialize bank:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn init --arg <ADMIN_ADDRESS>

User Authentication

Deposit with authentication:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn deposit --arg <USER1> --arg 1000 --sign-with-key <USER1_KEY>

Get balance:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn get_balance --arg <USER1>

Expected: 1000

Unauthorized deposit attempt (wrong account):

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn deposit --arg <USER2> --arg 500 --sign-with-key <USER1_KEY>

Expected error: Unauthorized (1)

Transfer with Authentication

Successful transfer:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn transfer --arg <USER1> --arg <USER2> --arg 300 --sign-with-key <USER1_KEY>

Verify balances:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn get_balance --arg <USER1>

Expected: 700

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn get_balance --arg <USER2>

Expected: 300

Admin Operations

Admin reset (authorized):

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn admin_reset_balance --arg <ADMIN> --arg <USER1> --sign-with-key <ADMIN_KEY>

Verify reset:

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn get_balance --arg <USER1>

Expected: 0

Admin reset (unauthorized):

soroban contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> --fn admin_reset_balance --arg <USER2> --arg <USER1> --sign-with-key <USER2_KEY>

Expected error: Unauthorized (1)

Step 5: Validation Checklist

✅ Contract initializes with admin ✅ Users can only access their own accounts ✅ Deposits and withdrawals work correctly ✅ Transfers between accounts succeed ✅ Admin functions are protected ✅ Unauthorized access is rejected ✅ All balance checks are enforced

Authentication Patterns

Pattern 1: Caller Verification

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
caller.require_auth();
}

Pattern 2: Role-Based Access

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let stored_admin: Address = env.storage()
    .instance()
    .get(&ADMIN)?;

if caller != stored_admin {
    return Err(ContractError::Unauthorized);
}
}

Pattern 3: Delegated Authority

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Function can be called by owner on behalf of user
pub fn transfer_for_user(
    env: Env,
    delegated_caller: Address,
    user: Address,
    amount: u128,
) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
    delegated_caller.require_auth();
    // ...
}
}

Security Best Practices

  1. Always Verify: Use require_auth() before sensitive operations
  2. Single Responsibility: One check per function
  3. Explicit Permissions: State clearly who can do what
  4. Audit Logging: Consider logging who did what
  5. Rate Limiting: Protect against abuse (advanced)

Common Pitfalls

  • Forgetting require_auth() calls
  • Mixing up caller with argument address
  • Not checking role/permission level
  • Replay attacks (Soroban handles this)

Troubleshooting

Issue: “Unauthorized” on valid calls

  • Solution: Ensure correct account is calling, check signature

Issue: Admin checks not working

  • Solution: Verify admin address in storage matches caller

Issue: Transfer fails unexpectedly

  • Solution: Check both accounts have sufficient balance

Advanced Topics

  • Multi-sig authorization
  • Time-locked transactions
  • Delegation patterns
  • Escrow mechanisms

Playground Tutorial 5: Multi-Contract Interactions

Overview

Learn how to build complex systems by having contracts interact with other contracts. This is essential for building DeFi applications.

Duration: 35-40 minutes Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Tutorials 1-4 completion

Learning Objectives

  • Pass contract addresses as parameters
  • Handle cross-contract errors

Step 1: Understanding Cross-Contract Communication

  • Call functions in deployed contracts
  • Pass contract addresses as parameters
  • Handle errors from called contracts
  • Design clear interfaces using traits

fn main() {

Step 3: Create a DEX Contract That Uses Tokens

Build a contract that calls the token contract:

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{
    contract, contractimpl, Address, Env, Symbol, symbol_short,
};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
#[repr(u32)]
pub enum ContractError {
    InvalidAmount = 1,
    InsufficientBalance = 2,
    PriceSlippage = 3,
    TokenTransferFailed = 4,
    InvalidPair = 5,
}

impl Into<u32> for ContractError {
    fn into(self) -> u32 {
        self as u32
    }
}

#[contract]
pub struct DexContract;

const LIQUIDITY_KEY: Symbol = symbol_short!("liq");
const PRICE_KEY: Symbol = symbol_short!("price");

#[contractimpl]
impl DexContract {
    /// Initialize liquidity pool
    pub fn init(
        env: Env,
        token_a: Address,
        token_b: Address,
        reserve_a: u128,
        reserve_b: u128,
    ) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
        // Validate amounts
        if reserve_a == 0 || reserve_b == 0 {
            return Err(ContractError::InvalidAmount);
        }
        
        // Store pool info
        env.storage()
            .instance()
            .set(&symbol_short!("tok_a"), &token_a);
        env.storage()
            .instance()
            .set(&symbol_short!("tok_b"), &token_b);
        env.storage()
            .instance()
            .set(&symbol_short!("res_a"), &reserve_a);
        env.storage()
            .instance()
            .set(&symbol_short!("res_b"), &reserve_b);
        
        // Calculate price ratio
        let price = (reserve_b as f64) / (reserve_a as f64);
        
        Ok(())
    }
    
    /// Execute a swap
    pub fn swap(
        env: Env,
        caller: Address,
        amount_in: u128,
        min_amount_out: u128,
        token_in: Address,
        token_out: Address,
    ) -> Result<u128, ContractError> {
        // Verify caller
        caller.require_auth();
        
        // Validate amounts
        if amount_in == 0 || min_amount_out == 0 {
            return Err(ContractError::InvalidAmount);
        }
        
        // Get pool reserves
        let reserve_a: u128 = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&symbol_short!("res_a"))
            .ok_or(ContractError::InvalidPair)?
            .map_err(|_| ContractError::InvalidPair)?;
        
        let reserve_b: u128 = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&symbol_short!("res_b"))
            .ok_or(ContractError::InvalidPair)?
            .map_err(|_| ContractError::InvalidPair)?;
        
        // Calculate output amount (simplified formula)
        // amount_out = (amount_in * reserve_b) / (reserve_a + amount_in)
        let amount_out = (amount_in as u128)
            .checked_mul(reserve_b)
            .ok_or(ContractError::InvalidAmount)?
            / (reserve_a + amount_in);
        
        // Check minimum output
        if amount_out < min_amount_out {
            return Err(ContractError::PriceSlippage);
        }
        
        // Transfer input tokens from caller to contract
        // This would call the token contract
        // token_in.transfer(caller, contract_address, amount_in)?;
        
        // Update reserves
        let new_reserve_a = reserve_a + amount_in;
        let new_reserve_b = reserve_b - amount_out;
        
        env.storage()
            .instance()
            .set(&symbol_short!("res_a"), &new_reserve_a);
        env.storage()
            .instance()
            .set(&symbol_short!("res_b"), &new_reserve_b);
        
        // Transfer output tokens to caller
        // token_out.transfer(contract_address, caller, amount_out)?;
        
        Ok(amount_out)
    }
    
    /// Get swap price
    pub fn get_price(
        env: Env,
        amount_in: u128,
    ) -> Result<u128, ContractError> {
        if amount_in == 0 {
            return Err(ContractError::InvalidAmount);
        }
        
        let reserve_a: u128 = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&symbol_short!("res_a"))
            .ok_or(ContractError::InvalidPair)?
            .map_err(|_| ContractError::InvalidPair)?;
        
        let reserve_b: u128 = env.storage()
            .instance()
            .get(&symbol_short!("res_b"))
            .ok_or(ContractError::InvalidPair)?
            .map_err(|_| ContractError::InvalidPair)?;
        
        let price = (amount_in as u128)
            .checked_mul(reserve_b)
            .ok_or(ContractError::InvalidAmount)?
            / (reserve_a + amount_in);
        
        Ok(price)
    }
    
    /// Add liquidity to pool
    pub fn add_liquidity(
        env: Env,
        provider: Address,
        amount_a: u128,
        amount_b: u128,
    ) -> Result<u128, ContractError> {
        provider.require_auth();
        
        if amount_a == 0 || amount_b == 0 {
            return Err(ContractError::InvalidAmount);
        }
        
        // Simplified: just return amount_a as LP tokens
        Ok(amount_a)
    }
}
}

Step 4: Build and Deploy Both Contracts

  1. Build both contracts:

    cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release

  2. Deploy token contract:

    soroban contract deploy --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/token_contract.wasm

    Save the contract ID as TOKEN_ID

  3. Deploy DEX contract:

    soroban contract deploy --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/dex_contract.wasm

    Save the contract ID as DEX_ID

Initialize the Pool

soroban contract invoke --id <DEX_ID> --fn init \
  --arg <TOKEN_ID> \
  --arg <USDC_ID> \
  --arg 1000000 \
  --arg 1000000

Get Price Quote

Execute Swap

  --arg <TOKEN_ID> \

  --arg 500000 \
  --arg 500000 \
  --sign-with-key <PROVIDER_KEY>

Step 6: Validation Checklist

✅ Both contracts deploy successfully ✅ DEX contract initializes with token addresses ✅ Price calculation returns correct values ✅ Swap executes with proper reserve updates ✅ Liquidity addition works correctly ✅ All error cases are handled ✅ Cross-contract calls complete without errors

Multi-Contract Patterns

Pattern 1: Contract Address as Parameter

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn swap(
    env: Env,
    token_in: Address,
    token_out: Address,
    amount: u128,
) -> Result<u128, ContractError> {
    // Can be called with any token address
}
}

Pattern 2: Inter-Contract Call

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Call another contract's function
let client = TokenClient::new(&env, &token_address);
let balance = client.balance_of(&caller);
}

Pattern 3: Error Propagation

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
match token.transfer(from, to, amount) {
    Ok(result) => Ok(result),
    Err(e) => Err(ContractError::TokenTransferFailed),
}
}

Best Practices

  1. Define Interfaces: Use traits for consistent contract APIs
  2. Error Handling: Wrap external calls in error handlers
  3. Validation: Verify all addresses before use
  4. Atomicity: Ensure all-or-nothing execution
  5. Security: Be careful with delegated authority

Security Considerations

  • Reentrancy: Soroban handles this for you
  • Price Slippage: Always enforce minimum output
  • Front-Running: Use mechanisms like batching
  • Contract Upgrades: Design for evolution
  • Emergency Stops: Consider pause mechanisms

Advanced Topics

  • Factory contracts for dynamic creation
  • Proxy patterns for upgradability
  • Batch operations
  • Flash loans and atomic swaps
  • Collateralized lending

Troubleshooting

Issue: “Contract not found”

  • Solution: Ensure contract ID is correct and deployed

Issue: “Invalid argument type”

  • Solution: Check address format and type matching

Issue: Swap always fails

  • Solution: Verify liquidity exists and prices are reasonable

fn main() {
// Persistent: Per-key TTL
env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &value);
env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&key, 100, 100);

// Instance: Shared TTL for all instance data
env.storage().instance().set(&key, &value);
env.storage().instance().extend_ttl(100, 100);

// Temporary: Ephemeral, no rent
env.storage().temporary().set(&key, &value);
}

03 Authentication

View Source

Live Demo

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Owner grants spender the right to move up to 500 tokens.
pub fn approve(env: Env, from: Address, spender: Address, amount: i128)
    -> Result<(), AuthError>
{
    from.require_auth();                                    // owner signs
    env.storage().persistent()
        .set(&DataKey::Allowance(from, spender), &amount);
    Ok(())
}

// Spender exercises the allowance.
pub fn transfer_from(
    env: Env, spender: Address, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128,
) -> Result<(), AuthError> {
    spender.require_auth();                                 // spender signs
    let allowance: i128 = env.storage().persistent()
        .get(&DataKey::Allowance(from.clone(), spender.clone()))
        .unwrap_or(0);
    if allowance < amount { return Err(AuthError::Unauthorized); }
    // â€¦ update balances and reduce allowance â€¦
    Ok(())
}
}

# One-time setup inside the Codespace
cargo install --locked soroban-cli

cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release
CONTRACT_ID=$(soroban contract deploy \
  --wasm ../../../target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/hello_world.wasm \
  --source alice \
  --network testnet)

# Call it

Every time you edit src/lib.rs, repeat the build and deploy commands to get a new contract ID running your latest code.

Example 01 — Hello World

Concepts: #[contract], #[contractimpl], Env, Symbol, Vec, symbol_short!

The simplest possible Soroban contract. It receives a name and returns a greeting vector. A great starting point for understanding how contracts are structured.

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]

fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, symbol_short, vec, Env, Symbol, Vec};

#[contract]
pub struct HelloContract;

#[contractimpl]
impl HelloContract {
    /// Returns ["Hello", <to>] as a Vec<Symbol>.
    pub fn hello(env: Env, to: Symbol) -> Vec<Symbol> {
        vec![&env, symbol_short!("Hello"), to]
    }
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/basics/01-hello-world
cargo test

What to edit: Change symbol_short!("Hello") to symbol_short!("Hola") and re-run the tests — watch one assertion fail and learn how to fix it.

Key concepts:

  • #[contract] marks the struct as a deployable contract unit.
  • #[contractimpl] exposes public functions as callable entry points.
  • Env is always the first parameter; it provides access to storage, events, and ledger.
  • symbol_short! creates a Symbol from a string literal of up to 9 characters.

Example 02 — Storage Patterns

Concepts: Persistent, Instance, and Temporary storage; TTL management; #[contracttype]

Soroban has three storage tiers with different lifetimes and costs. This example covers all three in one contract.

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]

fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, symbol_short, Env, Symbol};

#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum DataKey {
    Persistent(Symbol),
    Temporary(Symbol),
    Instance(Symbol),
}

#[contract]
pub struct StorageContract;

#[contractimpl]
impl StorageContract {
    // Persistent: survives upgrades; requires per-key TTL management.
    pub fn set_persistent(env: Env, key: Symbol, value: u64) {
        let storage_key = DataKey::Persistent(key.clone());
        env.storage().persistent().set(&storage_key, &value);
        env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&storage_key, 1000, 10000);
        env.events().publish(
            (symbol_short!("persist"), symbol_short!("set")),
            (key, value),
        );
    }

    pub fn get_persistent(env: Env, key: Symbol) -> Option<u64> {
        env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Persistent(key))
    }

    // Instance: tied to the contract instance lifetime; shared TTL.
    pub fn set_instance(env: Env, key: Symbol, value: u64) {
        env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Instance(key.clone()), &value);
        env.storage().instance().extend_ttl(1000, 10000);
    }

    pub fn get_instance(env: Env, key: Symbol) -> Option<u64> {
        env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Instance(key))
    }

    // Temporary: single-ledger lifetime; lowest cost; no TTL needed.
    pub fn set_temporary(env: Env, key: Symbol, value: u64) {
        env.storage().temporary().set(&DataKey::Temporary(key.clone()), &value);
    }

    pub fn get_temporary(env: Env, key: Symbol) -> Option<u64> {
        env.storage().temporary().get(&DataKey::Temporary(key))
    }
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/basics/02-storage-patterns
cargo test

What to edit: Remove the extend_ttl call from set_persistent and observe that the TTL-related tests fail — this demonstrates why TTL management matters.

Storage cheat-sheet:

TypeLifetimeCostBest for
PersistentUntil TTL expiresHighBalances, ownership
InstanceContract instanceMediumAdmin config, fees
TemporaryCurrent ledgerLowestReentrancy guards, caches

Example 03 — Custom Errors

Concepts: #[contracterror], Result<T, E>, error codes, structured error handling

Soroban contracts return typed errors via Rust’s Result. Using #[contracterror] assigns each variant a stable integer code that clients can match on.

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]

fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, Address, Env, Symbol};

#[contracterror]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
#[repr(u32)]
pub enum ContractError {
    InvalidInput        = 1,
    Unauthorized        = 2,
    NotFound            = 3,
    InsufficientBalance = 4,
    OperationNotAllowed = 5,
    RateLimitExceeded   = 6,
    ContractPaused      = 7,
    AlreadyExists       = 8,
}

#[contract]
pub struct CustomErrorsContract;

#[contractimpl]
impl CustomErrorsContract {
    /// Returns InvalidInput if value <= 0.
    pub fn validate_input(_env: Env, value: i64) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
        if value <= 0 {
            Err(ContractError::InvalidInput)
        } else {
            Ok(())
        }
    }

    /// Returns Unauthorized if caller != admin.
    pub fn check_authorization(
        _env: Env,
        caller: Address,
        admin: Address,
    ) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
        if caller != admin {
            Err(ContractError::Unauthorized)
        } else {
            Ok(())
        }
    }

    /// Returns InsufficientBalance or InvalidInput on bad transfers.
    pub fn transfer_tokens(
        _env: Env,
        from_balance: u64,
        amount: u64,
    ) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
        if amount == 0 {
            Err(ContractError::InvalidInput)
        } else if from_balance < amount {
            Err(ContractError::InsufficientBalance)
        } else {
            Ok(())
        }
    }
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/basics/03-custom-errors
cargo test

What to edit: Add a new variant Overflow = 9 to ContractError, then write a function that triggers it when two numbers would exceed u64::MAX.

Example 04 — Authentication

Concepts: require_auth(), admin patterns, RBAC, timelocks, allowances

require_auth() is Soroban’s core security primitive. Every state-mutating function that touches user funds should call it on the relevant address.

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]

fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env};

#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
#[repr(u32)]
pub enum Role { Admin = 0, Moderator = 1, User = 2 }

#[contracterror]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
#[repr(u32)]
pub enum AuthError {
    Unauthorized       = 1,
    NotAdmin           = 2,
    AlreadyInitialized = 3,
    InsufficientBalance = 4,
    TimeLocked         = 5,
    CooldownActive     = 6,
    InvalidState       = 7,
    InsufficientRole   = 8,
}

#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum DataKey { Admin, Balance(Address) }

#[contract]
pub struct AuthContract;

#[contractimpl]
impl AuthContract {
    /// One-time initialization — stores the admin address.
    pub fn initialize(env: Env, admin: Address) -> Result<(), AuthError> {
        if env.storage().instance().has(&DataKey::Admin) {
            return Err(AuthError::AlreadyInitialized);
        }
        admin.require_auth();
        env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Admin, &admin);
        Ok(())
    }

    /// Transfer tokens — `from` must authorize the call.
    pub fn transfer(env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), AuthError> {
        from.require_auth();    // <-- this is the core pattern

        let from_bal: i128 = env.storage().persistent()
            .get(&DataKey::Balance(from.clone())).unwrap_or(0);

        if from_bal < amount {
            return Err(AuthError::InsufficientBalance);
        }

        let to_bal: i128 = env.storage().persistent()
            .get(&DataKey::Balance(to.clone())).unwrap_or(0);

        env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Balance(from), &(from_bal - amount));
        env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Balance(to),   &(to_bal   + amount));
        Ok(())
    }

    pub fn get_balance(env: Env, user: Address) -> i128 {
        env.storage().persistent()
            .get(&DataKey::Balance(user)).unwrap_or(0)
    }
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/basics/03-authentication
cargo test

What to edit: Remove from.require_auth() from transfer and run the tests. The contract will no longer enforce ownership — a critical security hole.

Auth patterns in this example:

  • Basic require_auth() on the caller
  • Admin-only gates using a stored admin address
  • Role-based access control (Admin / Moderator / User)
  • Time-lock restrictions
  • Per-address cooldown periods
  • N-of-N multi-sig using require_auth() on a list

Example 05 — Events

Concepts: env.events().publish(), topic layout, indexed fields, structured payloads

Events are how Soroban contracts communicate state changes to off-chain consumers. Topics are indexed; the data payload is decoded after filtering.

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]

fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, symbol_short, Address, Env, Symbol};

#[contracttype]
pub struct TransferEventData {
    pub amount: i128,
    pub memo:   u64,
}

#[contract]
pub struct EventsContract;

#[contractimpl]
impl EventsContract {
    /// Emits a 4-topic transfer event.
    ///
    /// Topic layout:
    ///   [0] "events"    — namespace (filter all contract events)
    ///   [1] "transfer"  — action    (filter all transfers)
    ///   [2] sender      — indexed   (filter by sender)
    ///   [3] recipient   — indexed   (filter by recipient)
    ///   data: TransferEventData { amount, memo }
    pub fn transfer(env: Env, sender: Address, recipient: Address, amount: i128, memo: u64) {
        env.events().publish(
            (symbol_short!("events"), symbol_short!("transfer"), sender, recipient),
            TransferEventData { amount, memo },
        );
    }

    /// Emits a simple counter-increment event.
    pub fn increment(env: Env) {
        let mut num: u32 = env.storage().instance()
            .get(&symbol_short!("num")).unwrap_or(0);
        num += 1;
        env.storage().instance().set(&symbol_short!("num"), &num);
        env.events().publish(
            (symbol_short!("number"), symbol_short!("inc")),
            num,
        );
    }

    pub fn get_number(env: Env) -> u32 {
        env.storage().instance().get(&symbol_short!("num")).unwrap_or(0)
    }
}
}

Try it:

cd examples/basics/04-events
cargo test

What to edit: Add a second event inside increment that emits the previous value alongside the new value so off-chain consumers can detect the delta.

Topic design rules:

  • Put the most-filtered field in the earliest topic slot.
  • Max 4 topic slots per publish() call.
  • Prefer Symbol/Address in topics — they serialize cheaply.
  • Amounts and timestamps belong in data, not topics.

Example 06 — Error Handling (Result Propagation)

Concepts: Result<T, E>, ? operator, error chaining, #[contracterror]

cd examples/basics/05-error-handling
cargo test

Key pattern — use ? to propagate errors up the call stack without boilerplate:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn complex_operation(env: Env, amount: u64) -> Result<u64, ContractError> {
    validate_amount(amount)?;          // returns Err early if invalid
    let balance = load_balance(&env)?; // returns Err if not found
    Ok(balance - amount)
}
}

Example 07 — Auth Context

Concepts: require_auth_for_args(), sub-invocation authorization, call chains

cd examples/basics/05-auth-context
cargo test

Auth context lets a contract verify authorization for specific arguments, not just the bare caller identity:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Only authorizes this call if the user signed off on EXACTLY these args.
user.require_auth_for_args((&user, &amount).into_val(&env));
}

Example 08 — Validation Patterns

Concepts: Input validation, checked arithmetic, panic! vs Result

cd examples/basics/06-validation-patterns
cargo test

Core validation helpers:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Checked arithmetic prevents silent overflow
let result = a.checked_add(b).ok_or(ContractError::Overflow)?;

// Range check
if amount == 0 || amount > MAX_AMOUNT {
    return Err(ContractError::InvalidInput);
}
}

Example 09 — Type Conversions

Concepts: TryFromVal, IntoVal, Val, safe cross-boundary type handling

cd examples/basics/07-type-conversions
cargo test

Converting between Rust types and Soroban Val:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Convert a Rust type into a Val for storage or events
let val: Val = my_struct.into_val(&env);

// Convert back — returns Result, never panics
let my_struct = MyStruct::try_from_val(&env, &val)?;
}

Example 10 — Soroban Types

Concepts: Address, Symbol, Map, Vec, Bytes, BytesN

cd examples/basics/08-soroban-types
cargo test

Quick reference:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{Address, Bytes, BytesN, Map, Symbol, Vec};

// Symbol: short identifier ≤ 9 chars (compile-time)
let s = symbol_short!("hello");

// Map: key→value store living in host memory
let mut map: Map<Symbol, u64> = Map::new(&env);
map.set(symbol_short!("key"), 42u64);

// Vec: ordered list in host memory
let v: Vec<u64> = vec![&env, 1, 2, 3];

// BytesN: fixed-length byte array (e.g. 32-byte hash)
let hash: BytesN<32> = env.crypto().sha256(&data);
}

Example 11 — Enum Types

Concepts: #[contracttype] enums, state machines, dispatch tables

cd examples/basics/09-enum-types
cargo test

Use #[contracttype] enums as storage keys or contract state:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
pub enum Status { Active, Paused, Closed }

// Store state
env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Status, &Status::Active);

// Load and match
let status: Status = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Status)
    .unwrap_or(Status::Active);
match status {
    Status::Active => { /* normal operation */ }
    Status::Paused => return Err(ContractError::Paused),
    Status::Closed => return Err(ContractError::Closed),
}
}

Example 12 — Custom Structs

Concepts: #[contracttype] structs, composite storage keys, nested types

cd examples/basics/10-custom-structs
cargo test

Structs annotated with #[contracttype] can be stored directly and used as complex storage keys:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct UserProfile {
    pub name:    Symbol,
    pub balance: i128,
    pub tier:    u32,
}

// Use as a value
env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Profile(user.clone()), &profile);

// Use a tuple as a composite key
env.storage().persistent().set(&(owner.clone(), token_id), &metadata);
}

Example 13 — Primitive Types

Concepts: Integer overflow safety, u32/i128/u64, arithmetic patterns

cd examples/basics/11-primitive-types
cargo test

Soroban contracts compile with overflow-checks = true in release builds, so overflows panic rather than wrap. Use checked arithmetic for explicit handling:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Panics on overflow in debug; use checked_ for explicit Result
let safe = value.checked_mul(factor).ok_or(ContractError::Overflow)?;

// i128 is the canonical token amount type (128-bit signed integer)
pub fn transfer(_env: Env, amount: i128) { /* ... */ }
}

Example 14 — Data Types

Concepts: Full type system reference — Bytes, String, Map, Vec, tuples

cd examples/basics/12-data-types
cargo test

Soroban String is a host object — no format! or concatenation available:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::String;

// Create from a string literal
let s = String::from_str(&env, "hello world");

// Prefer Symbol for short identifiers (≤ 9 chars)
let sym = symbol_short!("hello");  // more gas-efficient than String
}

Example 15 — Collection Types

Concepts: Vec, Map, iteration, map merging, sorted access

cd examples/basics/13-collection-types
cargo test

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Vec — ordered, integer-indexed
let mut v: Vec<u64> = Vec::new(&env);
v.push_back(10);
v.push_back(20);
for item in v.iter() { /* ... */ }

// Map — unordered key→value
let mut m: Map<Address, u64> = Map::new(&env);
m.set(user.clone(), 100);
let val = m.get(user).unwrap_or(0);
}

Example 16 — Event Filtering

Concepts: Off-chain query patterns, topic ordering, indexer-friendly design

cd examples/basics/14-event-filtering
cargo test

Designing events that off-chain indexers can query efficiently:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Slot ordering matters for filter efficiency
env.events().publish(
    (
        symbol_short!("token"),   // [0] namespace  → "show me all token events"
        symbol_short!("transfer"),// [1] action     → "show me all transfers"
        from,                     // [2] primary    → "show me transfers FROM Alice"
        to,                       // [3] secondary  → "show me transfers TO Bob"
    ),
    amount,
);
}

Off-chain query progression (most → least broad):

  1. topic[0] == "token" — all contract events
  2. + topic[1] == "transfer" — all transfers
  3. + topic[2] == Alice — Alice’s outbound transfers
  4. + topic[3] == Bob — Alice-to-Bob transfers only

Troubleshooting

error[E0463]: can't find crate for std → Add the Wasm target: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown

error: package not found in workspace → Run the command from the workspace root, not from inside the example directory.

HostError: General during tests → You likely forgot env.mock_all_auths() before calling an auth-protected function.

extend_ttl panics in tests → This is expected when ledger sequence is 0. Wrap ledger setup with:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
env.ledger().with_mut(|li| { li.sequence_number = 100; li.timestamp = 1_000_000; });
}

Wasm binary is too large → Check Cargo.toml for opt-level = "z", lto = true, and strip = "symbols" in [profile.release].

Storage Patterns

Soroban’s three storage types — Persistent, Instance, and Temporary — offer different trade-offs for cost, lifetime, and use cases.

📊 Quick Comparison

FeaturePersistentInstanceTemporary
LifetimeSurvives upgrades, per-key TTLContract lifetimeSingle ledger
CostHighestMediumLowest
Use CasesUser balances, ownershipConfig, adminCaches, flags
TTLPer-keySharedPer-key (short)

🎯 When to Use What

Data > few ledgers? → Temporary
  ↓
Contract-wide config? → Instance  
  ↓
Per-user data → Persistent

Rules of Thumb:

  • Persistent: Token balances, votes
  • Instance: Admin address, fees
  • Temporary: Reentrancy guards, temp calc

💾 Code Example

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Persistent (extend TTL after write!)
env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &value);
env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&key, 100, 100);

// Instance (shared TTL)
env.storage().instance().set(&key, &value);
env.storage().instance().extend_ttl(100, 100);

// Temporary (no TTL needed)
env.storage().temporary().set(&key, &value);
}

Always check has() before get().unwrap_or(0) to avoid panics.

⚠️ Best Practices

  1. Extend TTL on writes (persistent/instance)
  2. Use enums for keys: #[contracttype] enum DataKey { Balance(Address) }
  3. Instance = small config only (loads all keys together)
  4. Threshold != 0 in extend_ttl (avoid redundant extensions)
  5. Compress only when helpful: compare raw and compressed storage sizes before storing large byte payloads. Compression can reduce rent for repetitive data, but may add cost for small or random payloads.

🔬 Full Example

examples/basics/02-storage-patterns/

Features:

  • All CRUD operations
  • TTL management
  • Isolation demo (same key in all 3 types)
  • Unit tests
  • Deployment instructions
  • Focused follow-up examples for instance storage, persistent storage, and temporary storage
  • Compressed storage examples for comparing raw vs encoded bytes

Error Handling

Master Soroban error patterns: custom errors, Result<T,E>, panic! best practices.

📊 Error Types Comparison

PatternUse WhenProsCons
Result<T, CustomError>Expected failures, user inputType-safe, frontend codes, cheapVerbose
panic!()Invariants, bugsSimpleWastes gas, poor UX
env.require_auth()Auth checksBuilt-inGeneric message

🎯 Best Practices

  1. Custom errors ≥8 variants w/ #[contracterror] + u32 codes
  2. Result<_, E> for business logic, panic! for invariants only
  3. Event on errors for debugging
  4. Test all paths w/ client.try_fn()
  5. Frontend mappable codes (1=InvalidInput, etc.)

💾 Key Code

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracterror]
#[repr(u32)]
pub enum Error {
    InvalidInput = 1, 
    Unauthorized = 2,
    // ...
}

pub fn transfer(env: Env, amount: u64) -> Result<(), Error> {
    if amount == 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidInput); }
    // ...
    Ok(())
}
}

Event Patterns

Soroban events consist of topics (indexed, filterable) and a data payload (non-indexed, arbitrary). Off-chain indexers filter by topic position; the data slot is decoded after a match.

env.events().publish(
    (topic_0, topic_1, topic_2, topic_3),  // up to 4 topics — indexed
    data_payload,                           // arbitrary SCVal — not indexed
);

📐 Topic Ordering Convention

All events in this cookbook follow a shared (namespace, action, [keys...]) layout:

SlotPurposeTypeNotes
[0]Contract namespaceSymbolAlways present. Identifies the contract.
[1]Action nameSymbolAlways present. Identifies the operation.
[2]Primary indexAddress/SymbolOptional. Most-queried entity.
[3]Secondary indexAddress/SymbolOptional. Second filter dimension.

Why this order? Off-chain indexers filter left-to-right. Putting the namespace first means a single topic filter catches every event from a contract. The action slot narrows to a category. Keys in slots 2–3 enable per-entity queries without scanning all events.

📊 Event Schemas by Category

1. Transfer Event

Tracks token movement between two parties.

SlotValueTypeIndexedRationale
[0]"events"Symbol✅Namespace filter — catch all contract events
[1]"transfer"Symbol✅Action filter — catch all transfers
[2]sender: AddressAddress✅Filter all sends from a wallet
[3]recipient: AddressAddress✅Filter all receives to a wallet
dataTransferEventDatastruct❌Amount + memo — read after topic match
 
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
pub struct TransferEventData {
    pub amount: i128,
    pub memo: u64,
}

env.events().publish(
    (symbol_short!("events"), symbol_short!("transfer"), sender, recipient),
    TransferEventData { amount, memo },
);
}

Off-chain query examples:

  • All transfers: topic[0] == "events" AND topic[1] == "transfer"
  • All sends by Alice: + topic[2] == Alice
  • Alice → Bob only: + topic[3] == Bob

2. Config Update Event

Tracks changes to contract configuration parameters.

SlotValueTypeIndexedRationale
[0]"events"Symbol✅Namespace filter
[1]"cfg_upd"Symbol✅Action filter — catch all config changes
[2]key: SymbolSymbol✅Filter changes to a specific parameter only
dataConfigUpdateEventDatastruct❌Old + new value — decoded after match
 
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
pub struct ConfigUpdateEventData {
    pub old_value: u64,
    pub new_value: u64,
}

env.events().publish(
    (symbol_short!("events"), symbol_short!("cfg_upd"), key),
    ConfigUpdateEventData { old_value, new_value },
);
}

Why key in topics? Consumers often monitor a specific parameter (e.g. "max_supply"). Putting it in slot [2] avoids decoding every config event just to check which parameter changed.

3. Admin Action Event

Tracks privileged operations for security monitoring.

SlotValueTypeIndexedRationale
[0]"events"Symbol✅Namespace filter
[1]"admin"Symbol✅Action filter — catch all admin operations
[2]admin: AddressAddress✅Filter actions by a specific admin address
dataAdminActionEventDatastruct❌Action symbol + timestamp — decoded after match
 
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
pub struct AdminActionEventData {
    pub action: Symbol,
    pub timestamp: u64,
}

env.events().publish(
    (symbol_short!("events"), symbol_short!("admin"), admin),
    AdminActionEventData { action, timestamp },
);
}

Why is action in data, not topics? Admin address (slot [2]) is the primary filter dimension for security monitoring. The specific action (pause, upgrade, etc.) is secondary context decoded after matching on the admin. Adding it as a 4th topic would consume the last slot with low query value.

4. Audit Trail Event

Full accountability log: who did what, captured for compliance.

SlotValueTypeIndexedRationale
[0]"events"Symbol✅Namespace filter
[1]"audit"Symbol✅Action filter — catch all audit entries
[2]actor: AddressAddress✅Filter all actions by a specific actor
[3]action: SymbolSymbol✅Filter a specific action type across all actors
dataAuditTrailEventDatastruct❌Details + timestamp + ledger sequence
 
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
pub struct AuditTrailEventData {
    pub details: Symbol,
    pub timestamp: u64,
    pub sequence: u32,
}

env.events().publish(
    (symbol_short!("events"), symbol_short!("audit"), actor, action),
    AuditTrailEventData { details, timestamp, sequence },
);
}

Why use all 4 topic slots here? Audit queries need two dimensions: who acted (actor) and what they did (action). Using both slots enables narrow queries like “all delete actions by Alice” without decoding payloads.

🎯 Indexed Field Rationale — Summary

Field typePut in topics?Reason
Entity addresses✅ YesMost-common filter dimension for wallets/contracts
Action/category✅ Yes (slot 1)Enables per-action subscriptions
Config key name✅ YesAvoids decoding payload just to check key name
Amounts❌ No (data)Rarely filtered; read after topic match
Timestamps❌ No (data)Range queries not supported on-chain anyway
Memo/details❌ No (data)Descriptive only; not a filter dimension

Rule of thumb: if an off-chain consumer would filter by this field to decide whether to process the event, it belongs in topics. If it’s only read after deciding to process the event, it belongs in data.

🎯 When To Emit

✅ State changes wallets/UI need (transfers, config updates) ✅ Admin operations (pause, upgrade, permission changes) ✅ Audit logs (who acted, when, on what) ❌ Internal calculations with no off-chain consumer ❌ High-frequency loops (avoid emitting 1000+ events per invocation)

⚡ Gas Considerations

  • Topics are cheaper than data per byte
  • Max 4 topic slots per event (contract address does not consume a slot)
  • Prefer Symbol / Address in topics — they serialise efficiently
  • Reserve the data slot for richer structs decoded after filtering

  • 4-topic transfers, config updates, admin actions, audit trails
  • Custom #[contracttype] payloads

Ajo Factory Pattern

The Contract Factory pattern is a powerful architectural design for Soroban smart contracts. It enables the creation of multiple isolated contract instances with identical logic but unique state.

📋 Overview

In traditional blockchain platforms like Ethereum, the “minimal proxy” (EIP-1167) pattern is used to save deployment costs by pointing to a single implementation. In Soroban, this is natively supported by separate storage and logic:

  1. Wasm Hash: You upload the contract’s binary once to the network.
  2. Deployer: The factory contract uses the env.deployer() interface to instantiate new contracts from that hash.
  3. Isolation: Each deployed instance has its own unique address and isolated storage.

🧠 Key Patterns

1. The Deployment Salt

Address derivation in Soroban is deterministic. To ensure each Ajo has its own address, the factory must provide a unique salt.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Combine creator address and counter to generate a unique salt
let salt = env.crypto().sha256(&(&creator, ajos.len()).into_val(&env));

let deployed_address = env
    .deployer()
    .with_current_contract(salt)
    .deploy(wasm_hash);
}

2. Initialization & Re-entrancy Protection

Since Soroban contracts are immutable once deployed, they use an initialize function. The factory contract must call this immediately to prevent anyone else from taking control of the instance.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Call initialize immediately after deployment
let ajo_client = AjoClient::new(&env, &deployed_address);
ajo_client.initialize(&amount, &max_members, &creator);
}

The Ajo contract itself should guard against multiple initializations:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
if env.storage().instance().has(&AjoDataKey::Creator) {
    panic!("Already initialized");
}
}

🛠️ Usage Example

Ajo Factory Logic

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn create_ajo(env: Env, amount: i128, max_members: u32, creator: Address) -> Address {
    creator.require_auth();

    let wasm_hash: BytesN<32> = env.storage().instance().get(&WasmHash).unwrap();

    // Deploy
    let deployed_address = env
        .deployer()
        .with_current_contract(salt)
        .deploy(wasm_hash);

    // Initialize
    let ajo_client = AjoClient::new(&env, &deployed_address);
    ajo_client.initialize(&amount, &max_members, &creator);

    deployed_address
}
}

🚀 Use Cases

  • Savings Groups (Ajos): Each group gets its own isolated ledger.
  • DAO Governance: Spawning individual proposal contracts.
  • Marketplace Escrows: Creating a fresh escrow contract for every trade.
  • Multi-tenant dApps: Isolating user state for security and independent TTL management.

🧪 Testing

The factory pattern is best tested by simulating the Wasm upload in your unit tests:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[test]
fn test_factory() {
    let env = Env::default();
    let wasm_hash = env.deployer().upload_contract_wasm(AjoWasm);
    // ... initialize factory and call create_ajo
}
}

Pause / Unpause

Administrative pause pattern for Soroban contracts.
