Security Pitfalls in Soroban Contracts

Soroban removes many classic EVM hazards by design, but it introduces its own sharp edges: host-enforced authorization, three distinct storage types with independent TTLs, and a host that reverts the whole call tree on panic. This page collects the mistakes that keep showing up in real Soroban deployments, with a vulnerable snippet, a fixed snippet, and the prevention rule for each one.

Read this alongside Security Best Practices, Common Pitfalls, and the Audit Checklist.

Table of Contents

  1. Threat model in 60 seconds
  2. Authorization pitfalls
  3. Cross-contract call pitfalls
  4. Reentrancy and read-only reentrancy
  5. Math, overflow, and precision pitfalls
  6. Panics, traps, and lost error information
  7. Storage and TTL pitfalls
  8. Token and allowance pitfalls
  9. Randomness, time, and oracle pitfalls
  10. Upgrade and proxy pitfalls
  11. Prevention strategy
  12. Pre-merge review checklist

1. Threat model in 60 seconds

Before listing pitfalls, be precise about who can do what:

  • A caller is an Address. A contract never “is trusted” because it was deployed earlier; every contract is untrusted code that happens to be deterministic.
  • require_auth() is checked by the host, not by your contract. A missing check is not “weaker validation”, it is no validation at all.
  • Any contract that calls your contract may be adversarial, including a contract you wrote, a token wrapper, or an oracle you integrate with.
  • Storage is keyed by contract ID. Instance and temporary entries are separate namespaces from persistent entries, and temporary entries are wiped between ledger close and the next protocol upgrade rotation.

The three questions to ask about every entry point are:

  1. Who is allowed to call this, and how is that enforced?
  2. What state is read, and what state is written, in what order?
  3. Whose code runs during this call, and can it call me back?

2. Authorization pitfalls

2.1 Missing require_auth() on a state-changing function

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// VULNERABLE: anyone can pass another user's address
pub fn withdraw(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) {
    let mut balance = get_balance(&env, &user);
    balance -= amount;
    set_balance(&env, &user, balance);
}
}
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// FIXED
pub fn withdraw(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) {
    user.require_auth();
    let balance = get_balance(&env, &user);
    let new_balance = balance
        .checked_sub(amount)
        .ok_or(Error::InsufficientBalance)?;
    set_balance(&env, &user, new_balance);
    env.events().publish((symbol_short!("withdraw"), user.clone()), amount);
}
}

Prevention: call require_auth() as the first statement of every function that mutates state or moves value, and prefer require_auth_for_args when the signature covers only part of the operation.

2.2 Authorizing a contract address you do not control

require_auth() on an address that is a contract means that contract’s __check_auth must approve. If that contract’s implementation is an open proxy or has a permissive fallback, your authorization is effectively public.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// VULNERABLE: authorization delegated to an arbitrary caller-supplied address
pub fn sweep(env: Env, caller: Address, to: Address, amount: i128) {
    caller.require_auth();
    token_client.transfer(&caller, &to, &amount);
}
}
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// FIXED: an authorized admin is stored in instance storage and may not be changed
// without a timelock
fn admin(env: &Env) -> Address {
    env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Admin).unwrap()
}

pub fn sweep(env: Env, to: Address, amount: i128) {
    admin(&env).require_auth();
    if to == env.current_contract_address() {
        return Err(Error::InvalidRecipient.into());
    }
    let token = token_address(&env);
    token::Client::new(&env, &token).transfer(&admin(&env), &to, &amount);
    Ok(())
}
}

Prevention: store the authority that may call an entry point in storage, load it inside the function, and require auth on the loaded value. Never authorize a caller-supplied address for an operation the caller should not be able to route.

2.3 Auth inside a loop, or only on the happy path

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// VULNERABLE: early returns and `continue` skip authorization for later items
pub fn settle(env: Env, claims: Vec<(Address, i128)>) {
    for (to, amount) in claims.iter() {
        if amount == &0 {
            continue; // never authorized
        }
        // ...
    }
}
}

Prevention: authenticate once at the top of the function, before any branching or looping, for every address the function can act on behalf of.

2.4 Confusing require_auth with require_auth_for_args

require_auth() demands that the whole Address payload of the invocation be authorized. require_auth_for_args(...) authorizes only the listed values, which is correct for a function with a non-signing caller parameter.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// VULNERABLE: requires the user to sign the admin address too, which is impossible
pub fn transfer_from_admin(env: Env, user: Address, admin: Address, amount: i128) {
    user.require_auth();
    admin.require_auth();
    move_funds(&env, &admin, &user, amount);
}
}

Prevention: if a parameter only identifies what is being changed and the signer is someone else, authorize only the signer and validate the rest against stored state.

2.5 Replay through shared invocations

Soroban supports sub-invocations, so a contract can request your contract to act inside someone else’s transaction. If your entry point relies on “the direct caller is the user”, a malicious contract can call it on the user’s behalf.

Prevention: use env.invoker() for caller checks when the semantics require the immediate invoker, and use require_auth() for identity checks. Pick one deliberately; do not mix them implicitly.

3. Cross-contract call pitfalls

3.1 Trusting the callee to enforce your invariants

A token contract that does not revert on a zero-amount transfer will happily return Ok. If your accounting assumes failure, it silently drifts.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// VULNERABLE: assumes a failed transfer reverts
pub fn deposit(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> {
    token_client.transfer(&user, &env.current_contract_address(), &amount);
    credit(&env, &user, amount); // credited even if the token silently no-ops
    Ok(())
}
}
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// FIXED: observe the balance delta, do not trust the return value alone
pub fn deposit(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let token = token_address(&env);
    let contract = env.current_contract_address();
    let client = token::Client::new(&env, &token);
    let before = client.balance(&contract);

    client.transfer(&user, &contract, &amount);

    let received = client
        .balance(&contract)
        .checked_sub(before)
        .ok_or(Error::AmountMismatch)?;
    if received != amount {
        return Err(Error::AmountMismatch);
    }
    credit(&env, &user, received);
    Ok(())
}
}

Prevention: for fee-on-transfer and rebasing-style assets, reconcile against an observed balance change. Never assume amount arrived.

3.2 Unchecked try_ results

try_invoke_contract and try_transfer return Result instead of trapping. Swallowing it converts a failure into an inconsistent success.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// VULNERABLE
let _ = token_client.try_transfer(&from, &to, &amount);

// FIXED
token_client.try_transfer(&from, &to, &amount).map_err(|_| Error::TransferFailed)?;
}

Prevention: propagate every Result with ? or an explicit match. A let _ = on a call that moves value should be treated as a review blocker.

3.3 Unbounded loops over caller-controlled input

A Vec argument with 10,000 entries costs 10,000 ledger reads and can exceed the CPU budget, failing for every legitimate user while a griefing caller pays almost nothing.

Prevention: bound loop inputs (if items.len() > MAX_BATCH { return Err(...) }), prefer batching helpers that take fixed-size arrays, and keep external calls out of loops.

4. Reentrancy and read-only reentrancy

Soroban does not allow a contract to be re-entered while it is already on the call stack, which removes direct self-reentrancy. It does not remove cross-contract reentrancy: A -> B -> A is legal as long as the inner A invocation starts from a fresh frame in the same transaction, and it also does not stop read-only reentrancy, where B calls a view function on A while A is mid-update and observes half-updated state.

4.1 The vulnerable shape

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// VULNERABLE: state is read *after* an external call
pub fn withdraw(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) {
    let balance = get_balance(&env, &user);
    token_client.transfer(&env.current_contract_address(), &user, amount);
    set_balance(&env, &user, balance - amount); // balance may be stale
}
}

4.2 Fix 1: checks-effects-interactions

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// FIXED: write state first, interact last
pub fn withdraw(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> {
    user.require_auth();

    let balance = get_balance(&env, &user);
    let remaining = balance
        .checked_sub(amount)
        .ok_or(Error::InsufficientBalance)?;
    set_balance(&env, &user, remaining);

    let token = token_address(&env);
    token::Client::new(&env, &token).transfer(
        &env.current_contract_address(),
        &user,
        &amount,
    );
    Ok(())
}
}

4.3 Fix 2: an explicit reentrancy guard

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn set_entered(env: &Env, entered: bool) {
    let key = DataKey::Entered;
    if entered {
        env.storage().temporary().set(&key, &true);
    } else {
        env.storage().temporary().remove(&key);
    }
}

fn guard(env: &Env) -> Result<(), Error> {
    if env.storage().temporary().has(&DataKey::Entered) {
        return Err(Error::Reentrancy);
    }
    set_entered(env, true);
    Ok(())
}

pub fn guarded_withdraw(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> {
    guard(&env)?;
    // ... effects and interactions ...
    set_entered(&env, false);
    Ok(())
}
}

Use a temporary entry for the flag: it is the cheapest storage and it is reset at ledger close, so a panic mid-function cannot leave the contract locked for the next transaction.

4.4 Read-only reentrancy

If get_* functions read several keys and a callee can call them mid-update, the callee sees inconsistent state and can price against it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// FIXED: a read guard makes views refuse to answer mid-update
pub fn get_position(env: Env, user: Address) -> Result<(i128, i128), Error> {
    if env.storage().temporary().has(&DataKey::Entered) {
        return Err(Error::Reentrancy);
    }
    Ok((get_balance(&env, &user), get_collateral(&env, &user)))
}
}

Prevention rules

  1. Apply checks-effects-interactions everywhere; treat the guard as defense in depth, not as the primary protection.
  2. Keep external calls in the last statements of the function.
  3. Guard views that aggregate state when the contract can be called back into.
  4. Add a regression test that performs the A -> B -> A cycle and asserts the inner call fails.

See examples/advanced/15-reentrancy-guard for a runnable version of all three defenses.

5. Math, overflow, and precision pitfalls

5.1 Unchecked arithmetic in release builds

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// VULNERABLE: wraps or traps depending on the profile
pub fn accrue(env: Env, user: Address) {
    let balance = get_balance(&env, &user);
    set_balance(&env, &user, balance * 2);
}
}
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// FIXED
pub fn accrue(env: Env, user: Address) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let balance = get_balance(&env, &user);
    let doubled = balance.checked_mul(2).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?;
    set_balance(&env, &user, doubled);
    Ok(())
}
}

Prevention: every arithmetic result that touches a balance, a price, or a share uses checked_*. Add a #![deny(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]-style lint gate, or enable clippy::indexing_slicing and clippy::arithmetic_side_effects in the workspace lint configuration.

5.2 Integer division truncation

(a + b) / 2 rounds toward zero and silently favours one side. In share math and fee distribution this creates a rounding gap that accumulates.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// VULNERABLE: the remainder is lost
let half = (a + b) / 2;

// FIXED: multiply by a large scalar and divide last (Soroban recipe)
const SCALE: i128 = 1_000_000;
let half = ((a + b) * SCALE / 2) / SCALE;
}

Prevention: follow the Soroban SDK “integer without floating point” recipe - scale up, divide, scale down - and document the rounding direction in a comment.

5.3 Sign confusion between i128 and u128

Amounts that can be negative (signed) and amounts that cannot (unsigned) get mixed, and casting silently wraps.

Prevention: pick one type for amounts (usually i128), forbid as casts in review, and use TryFrom/TryInto where a conversion is genuinely needed.

6. Panics, traps, and lost error information

A Soroban panic aborts the entire transaction and consumes all gas, so a stray unwrap() is a denial-of-service bug for that user, not just a crash.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// VULNERABLE
let balance = get_balance(&env, &user).unwrap(); // panics when the key is absent

// FIXED
let balance = get_balance(&env, &user).unwrap_or(0);
}

Other traps to watch for:

  • symbol_short! panics above 9 characters; Symbol::new panics above 32.
  • Indexing a Vec or Map out of bounds panics; use get().
  • Arithmetic overflow in a debug test but wraparound in a release WASM - the bug reproduces only in the artifact you shipped.
  • env.storage().instance().get(...).unwrap() after a failed initialization path.

Prevention: define a #[contracttype] enum Error, return Result from every external entry point, and reserve panics for genuine invariants.

7. Storage and TTL pitfalls

Storage mistakes are security bugs because they become permission bugs.

PitfallConsequenceFix
Writing a balance to temporary storageBalance vanishes at ledger closePersistent + extend_ttl
Extending TTL only on writeLong-idle keys expire under the userExtend on read too
Same key name in two storage typesSilent split brainNamespaced enum keys
instance() used for a growing mapEvery call loads the whole mapPersistent per-entry keys
Unbounded key growthState bloat, expensive snapshotsPrune or archive off-chain
 
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// FIXED: persistent with a bounded extension, checked on both write and read
pub fn set_balance(env: &Env, user: &Address, amount: i128) {
    let key = DataKey::Balance(user.clone());
    env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &amount);
    env.storage()
        .persistent()
        .extend_ttl(&key, LEDGER_THRESHOLD, LEDGER_BUMP);
}

pub fn get_balance(env: &Env, user: &Address) -> i128 {
    let key = DataKey::Balance(user.clone());
    let value = env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0);
    env.storage()
        .persistent()
        .extend_ttl(&key, LEDGER_THRESHOLD, LEDGER_BUMP);
    value
}
}

Prevention: a single #[contracttype] enum DataKey per contract, one helper per stored concept, LEDGER_THRESHOLD/LEDGER_BUMP constants derived from your minimum viable TTL, and TTL extension on read paths that matter. The full treatment lives in Storage Pitfalls.

8. Token and allowance pitfalls

  • Approve-then-transfer race: a user who changes an allowance from 100 to 0 can be front-run by the spender using the old allowance. Provide a decrease_allowance helper and document the risk.
  • Infinite approvals to a contract you later upgrade are permanent exposures. Prefer exact allowances or pull-based patterns.
  • Hard-coded token addresses in code make upgrades impossible. Read the token from instance storage.
  • Rebasing or fee-on-transfer tokens break amount == received assumptions; reconcile against balance deltas.

9. Randomness, time, and oracle pitfalls

  • There is no secure randomness in a deterministic VM. env.random() is seeded by the protocol and is predictable to a caller who influences the inputs; never use it for lotteries, shuffles, or key generation.
  • env.ledger().timestamp() is producer-controlled within a window. Never use it as a precise deadline or as an entropy source.
  • Oracle prices are stale by design. Validate the price, bound it against a sanity range, and store the timestamp alongside the value.

10. Upgrade and proxy pitfalls

  • An upgradeable contract keeps its storage. Any layout change must be additive or accompanied by a migration function that runs once, guarded by a version marker in storage.
  • An uninitialized proxy can be initialized by an attacker and take permanent ownership. Set admin atomically in the initializer and re-initialization must revert.
  • Upgrading a contract whose keys are unnamespaced can collide with the new implementation’s keys.

Prevention: store a Version in instance storage, expose migrate() with a require_auth on a timelocked admin, and validate layouts before deploying (see examples/advanced/09-storage-layout-validator and examples/advanced/10-contract-migrations).

11. Prevention strategy

LayerAction
DesignThreat-model each entry point; write the abuse case next to the happy path
Key designOne DataKey enum; no ad-hoc Symbol/String keys
Authrequire_auth() first, on a stored address where possible
Arithmeticchecked_* everywhere; no as casts
External callsLast statement; results always checked
GuardsTemporary reentrancy flag + read guard for aggregators
ErrorsContract-defined Error enum; no unwrap() in entry points
Time to liveExtend on read and write; test with --durability scenarios
UpgradeVersion marker + tested migration path
ReviewTwo reviewers for auth and math changes; audit checklist

Testing checklist

  • A test where the caller is not the beneficiary must fail with an authorization error.
  • A test that drives A -> B -> A must show the inner call rejected.
  • A test that expires TTLs (test::with_budget plus a ledger bump simulation) must show balances intact.
  • A test that passes a fee-on-transfer style mock must show reconciliation.
  • Every try_* result is asserted, including the failure branch.

12. Pre-merge review checklist

  • Every state-changing entry point calls require_auth() on a trusted address
  • No unwrap() in any external entry point
  • No unchecked arithmetic on balances, prices, or shares
  • Every external call result handled; no let _ = on value-moving calls
  • Effects written before interactions
  • Reentrancy guard present where the contract can be called back into
  • View functions that aggregate state are guarded
  • Persistent storage for anything that must survive a ledger close
  • TTL extended on read and write paths
  • Storage keys namespaced by a DataKey enum
  • Proxy initializer cannot be run twice
  • Tests cover unauthorized, reentrant, and expired-TTL paths

Storage Pitfalls in Soroban Contracts

Soroban has no mapping and no storage keyword. Every byte a contract keeps lives in one of three storage namespaces with three different lifetimes and three different costs. Almost every storage bug in a Soroban contract is one of three things: the wrong namespace, the wrong key, or the wrong time to live (TTL) handling.

This page lists the mistakes that ship, the symptom each one produces, and the fix. Use it together with Storage Patterns, Common Pitfalls, and Security Pitfalls.

Table of Contents

  1. The three storage types
  2. Choosing the right type
  3. Storage type confusion
  4. Key design and key collisions
  5. TTL, rent, and liveness
  6. Bugs that only appear at expiration
  7. Migration problems
  8. Cost and performance traps
  9. Best practices
  10. Review checklist

1. The three storage types

PersistentInstanceTemporary
Namespaceenv.storage().persistent()env.storage().instance()env.storage().temporary()
LifetimeUntil the entry’s TTL expiresUntil the contract instance’s TTL expiresMinutes; restored at ledger close
TTL granularityPer keyShared across all instance entriesPer key, short
Intended useUser balances, positions, allowancesContract configurationLocks, caches, nonces
Relative rentHighestMediumLowest
Survives contract upgradeYesYes (instance survives a WASM update)No

Key facts that cause most of the bugs below:

  • Persistent entries each carry their own TTL. When a persistent entry expires, the contract is restored on the next invocation that touches it, and the entry has to pay the rent again.
  • Instance entries share a single TTL per key that is linked to the contract instance. Instance storage is also the account of the contract itself, so bumping the contract instance TTL and bumping an instance entry are separate operations.
  • Temporary entries are cheap precisely because they are short lived. They are restored during ledger close, they have a hard minimum TTL enforced by the protocol, and they are always cheaper per byte than persistent entries.

2. Choosing the right type

Does the value need to survive beyond a few ledgers?
├── yes → Does it belong to one user / position?
│         ├── yes → persistent, one entry per key, bump TTL on read and write
│         └── no  → instance (contract-wide config), keep it small
└── no  → temporary (reentrancy guard, per-transaction nonce, scratch value)

Rules of thumb:

  • Balances, allowances, positions, votes, and metadata URIs: persistent.
  • Admin address, fee basis points, oracle address, pause flag, token address: instance.
  • Reentrancy guard flag, “already used” nonces, transient computation results: temporary.

3. Storage type confusion

3.1 Balances in temporary storage

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// BROKEN: the balance disappears at ledger close / when the entry expires
pub fn deposit(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) {
    let key = DataKey::Balance(user.clone());
    env.storage().temporary().set(&key, &amount);
}
}

Symptom: deposits succeed, then reads return zero. Users lose funds; the integration tests pass because they never advance a ledger.

Fix: use persistent storage and bump the TTL.

3.2 Configuration in persistent storage

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// WORKS, but pays persistent rent for a value read on every call
pub fn set_admin(env: Env, admin: Address) {
    env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Admin, &admin);
}
}

Fix: instance storage. The admin is contract-wide state, so it belongs in the instance namespace and is loaded with the rest of the instance configuration.

3.3 Instance storage used as a database

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// BROKEN: a map grows inside the instance namespace
env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Users, &users_vec);
}

Fix: one persistent entry per user.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::User(user.clone()), &user_record);
}

Instance storage is intended for configuration that is small and bounded. Growing it increases the cost of every invocation and eventually makes the contract unusable.

3.4 Persistent storage used as a cache

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// EXPENSIVE: persistent rent for data that is only needed right now
let key = DataKey::Price(feed.clone());
env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &price);
}

Fix: keep the cache in temporary storage, or keep it in memory for the duration of the call. Persistent storage should hold state you cannot recompute.

3.5 Same key name in two namespaces

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
env.storage().persistent().set(&symbol_short!("config"), &config);
env.storage().instance().set(&symbol_short!("config"), &other_config);
}

Fix: never rely on the name to disambiguate. Use a DataKey enum whose variants are explicit, and never reuse one variant for two different concepts.

3.6 Reading from the wrong namespace after an upgrade

An upgrade that moves a value from one namespace to another looks fine in tests (fresh state) and fails in production (existing state).

Fix: when a release changes namespaces, ship a migration that reads from the old namespace and writes to the new one, and gate it behind a version marker.

4. Key design and key collisions

4.1 Ad-hoc keys instead of an enum

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// FRAGILE: two features can both decide that "fee" is a good key name
env.storage().instance().set(&Symbol::new(&env, "fee"), &fee);
env.storage().instance().set(&Symbol::new(&env, "fee"), &admin);
}

Fix: one #[contracttype] enum per contract.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum DataKey {
    Balance(Address),
    Allowance(Address, Address),
    Admin,
    FeeBps,
    Config,
}
}

4.2 Composite keys that flatten into each other

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// COLLISION: ("alice", "bob") can be produced by ("ali", "cebob")
env.storage().persistent().set(&(a.clone(), b.clone()), &value);
}

Fix: make the tuple shape unambiguous, or use distinct DataKey variants such as Allowance(Address, Address) and Position(Address, Symbol). The types must match at every call site, which is what prevents the mix-up.

4.3 Key length limits

symbol_short! panics above 9 characters and Symbol::new panics above 32. Long descriptive key strings panic at runtime, which means the whole transaction fails.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// PANICS: longer than 32 characters
let key = Symbol::new(&env, "user_registration_timestamp_for_active_pool");
}

Fix: short symbols for symbol_short!, an enum for anything structured.

4.4 Keys that expose implementation details

A key that embeds a value that can change (Balance keyed by a mutable address alias, or Config keyed by a version number that is bumped) breaks every reader that cached the old key.

Fix: keys are permanent identities. If the meaning changes, introduce a new key and migrate.

4.5 Confusing the contract instance with instance entries

The contract instance (the account that holds the WASM and the instance entries) has its own WasmHash and its own TTL, managed with the contract instance API. It is easy to write env.storage().instance() code that accidentally assumes contract-instance semantics, for example expecting it to be restored the same way.

Fix: be explicit about which one you mean: instance entries (env.storage().instance()), or the contract instance (the WasmHash and its lifetime).

5. TTL, rent, and liveness

Soroban storage is rented. An entry’s life is its TTL, expressed in ledgers.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
const LEDGER_THRESHOLD: u32 = 5_184_000; // ~6 months
const LEDGER_BUMP: u32 = 1_209_600;      // ~2 months
}

Typical patterns:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Bump on write
env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &value);
env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&key, LEDGER_THRESHOLD, LEDGER_BUMP);

// Bump on read, so active users never expire
let value = env.storage().persistent().get(&key);
env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&key, LEDGER_THRESHOLD, LEDGER_BUMP);
}

Pitfalls:

  • Only bumping on write. A user who deposits once and only withdraws months later loses their entry to expiration. Bump on read paths that matter.
  • Zero threshold. extend_ttl(&key, 0, 0) only restores an already-expired entry and is charged the restoration fee. Use a real threshold.
  • Unbounded threshold. An enormous threshold can be unaffordable; rent is charged for the entire extension.
  • Forgetting temporary storage needs no bump. Temporary entries have a protocol-enforced minimum TTL. Adding manual bump logic there is noise at best.
  • Instance TTL is extended with the instance. When the contract instance is restored or its lifetime is extended, its instance entries come along; do not assume every instance entry has an independent TTL.

6. Bugs that only appear at expiration

This is the classic Soroban storage bug class: the code is correct until a TTL runs out.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// BUG: an expired entry is indistinguishable from "never existed"
let balance = env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0);
}

If the entry expired and was restored as empty, unwrap_or(0) silently turns a user’s balance into zero. The same pattern turns a “not yet set” admin into a “no admin” contract, and a nonce into a reusable one.

Fixes:

  • For balances, decide explicitly whether “missing” means zero (a new user) or “corrupt state” (an expired entry), and return a contract error for the latter.

  • Test expiration. The SDK lets you advance the ledger sequence in tests so you can exercise the expired-entry path deliberately:

    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let seq = env.ledger().sequence();
env.ledger().with_mut(|li| li.sequence = seq + 10_000);
}

  • Restore the contract before reading: env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl on an expired entry charges the restoration fee, which is why it is not free.

7. Migration problems

Storage migrations are the highest-risk change a Soroban contract can make, because the ledger state is long lived and the contract code is short lived.

7.1 The rules

  1. Additive by default. New keys are safe. Renaming, retyping, or removing a key is not.
  2. Never reinterpret an existing key. If the meaning of a value changes, introduce a new key and a migration step; do not write a new type over the old value.
  3. Version everything. Store a version number in instance storage, and make migrate() idempotent: it should check the current version and do nothing if the contract is already migrated.
  4. Test the upgrade path, not just the fresh path. Write a test that writes state with the old layout, runs the migration, and asserts the new layout reads the migrated values.

7.2 A version marker and idempotent migration

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
const VERSION: u32 = 2;

#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum DataKey {
    Version,
    Config,
    Balance(Address),
}

fn version(env: &Env) -> u32 {
    env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Version).unwrap_or(1)
}

pub fn migrate(env: Env) -> Result<(), Error> {
    admin(&env).require_auth();

    match version(&env) {
        1 => migrate_v1_to_v2(&env),
        VERSION => return Ok(()), // already migrated: stay idempotent
        v => return Err(Error::UnsupportedVersion),
    }

    env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Version, &VERSION);
    Ok(())
}

fn migrate_v1_to_v2(env: &Env) {
    // Move the config from the old flat key to the new namespaced key.
    if let Some(old) = env.storage().persistent().get(&Symbol::new(env, "config")) {
        env.storage().persistent().remove(&Symbol::new(env, "config"));
        env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Config, &old);
    }
}
}

7.3 Upgrades versus migrations

Updating the contract WASM keeps the storage as it is. That is why:

  • init must not be re-runnable on an upgraded contract. Use a separate initialize entry point guarded by a “already initialized” check.
  • migrate must be callable by an authorized (ideally timelocked) admin only.
  • Layout validation before deploying a new WASM is worth automating. See examples/advanced/09-storage-layout-validator (schema compatibility rules) and examples/advanced/10-contract-migrations for runnable patterns.

8. Cost and performance traps

  • One entry per user, not one entry for all users. Each persistent() read is billed per entry touched.
  • Avoid extend_ttl in hot loops. Bumping TTL for 100 users in one call is 100 billed extensions. Bump on the entries that are actually being used.
  • Instance storage is loaded as a unit. A large instance entry slows down every call, including read-only calls.
  • Temporary storage for scratch space. Intermediate values that never need to persist belong in temporary storage or in ordinary Rust memory.
  • Prefer has() before get(). has is cheaper than a full read and makes the intent explicit.
  • Measure. The repo includes gas benchmarks under gas-benchmarks/ and a storage-focused example at examples/advanced/09-storage-optimization.

9. Best practices

  1. One DataKey enum per contract. No ad-hoc Symbol or String keys.

  2. One helper per stored concept, so TTL handling lives in exactly one place:

    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn set_balance(env: &Env, user: &Address, amount: i128) {
    let key = DataKey::Balance(user.clone());
    env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &amount);
    env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&key, LEDGER_THRESHOLD, LEDGER_BUMP);
}

fn get_balance(env: &Env, user: &Address) -> i128 {
    let key = DataKey::Balance(user.clone());
    let value = env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0);
    env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&key, LEDGER_THRESHOLD, LEDGER_BUMP);
    value
}
}

  3. Persistent for durable user state, instance for small bounded config, temporary for locks and scratch values.

  4. Bump TTL on both write and read, with a documented threshold and bump.

  5. Make migrate idempotent and version-gated; never reinterpret a key.

  6. Treat expiration as a test case. Advance the ledger sequence in tests and assert the behavior you expect.

  7. Prefer Option/Result over unwrap() so a missing entry is a handled branch rather than a panic that reverts the whole transaction.

  8. Keep instance storage small. Move anything that grows into persistent entries.

  9. Document each key with a comment describing its type, lifetime, and meaning. Storage keys are the contract’s real schema.

  10. Audit the layout before every upgrade, not just the code diff.

10. Review checklist

  • Every key comes from a DataKey enum; no inline symbols or strings
  • Balances and positions are persistent, not temporary
  • Instance storage holds only small, bounded configuration
  • Temporary storage holds only locks, nonces, and scratch values
  • TTL is extended on write and on the read paths that matter
  • extend_ttl uses a non-zero, affordable threshold
  • Missing entries are handled deliberately, not unwrap()-ed
  • An expiration test exists (ledger sequence advanced past the TTL)
  • Key tuples cannot collide with each other
  • migrate is idempotent, version-gated, and admin-authorized
  • The upgrade test starts from state written by the previous version
  • No key is renamed, retyped, or repurposed without a migration step

  • Security Pitfalls
  • Common Pitfalls

Common Pitfalls in Soroban Smart Contracts

This guide outlines the most common mistakes developers make when writing smart contracts for Soroban on Stellar. It covers both beginner-level issues (basic API usage, Rust quirks, and entry point rules) and intermediate-level design flaws (storage architecture, state archival, and security vulnerabilities).

🟢 Beginner Pitfalls

1. Missing Authorization Checks

  • Mistake: Passing an Address to a function and performing state changes or asset transfers on its behalf without verifying its authorization.
  • Consequence: Anyone can call the contract function and input another user’s address, allowing them to unauthorizedly spend funds or manipulate state.
  • How to avoid/fix: Always invoke .require_auth() on the Address parameter representing the signer.
  • Code Example: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// ❌ BAD: Anyone can call this function and pass another user's address
pub fn withdraw(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) {
    let mut balance = get_balance(&env, &user);
    balance -= amount;
    set_balance(&env, &user, balance);
}

// ✅ GOOD: Verifies that the transaction was signed by the user
pub fn withdraw(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) {
    user.require_auth();
    let mut balance = get_balance(&env, &user);
    balance -= amount;
    set_balance(&env, &user, balance);
}
}

2. Unchecked Arithmetic (Integer Overflow/Underflow)

  • Mistake: Using standard mathematical operators (+, -, *, /) for calculating token balances or values.
  • Consequence: In release builds, overflow checks might wrap around silently (if they are disabled in the profile), leading to exploit vectors such as minting massive numbers of tokens. Even if checks are enabled, standard operators panic without providing a clear error code, making error handling impossible.
  • How to avoid/fix: Use checked arithmetic methods (checked_add, checked_sub, checked_mul, checked_div) and return custom, descriptive contract errors.
  • Code Example: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// ❌ BAD: Standard operator can cause panics or wrap-around exploits
pub fn add_interest(balance: u64, rate: u64) -> u64 {
    balance + (balance * rate) / 100
}

// ✅ GOOD: Checked math returning custom error types
pub fn add_interest(balance: u64, rate: u64) -> Result<u64, Error> {
    let interest = balance
        .checked_mul(rate)
        .ok_or(Error::ArithmeticOverflow)?
        .checked_div(100)
        .ok_or(Error::ArithmeticOverflow)?;
    
    balance.checked_add(interest).ok_or(Error::ArithmeticOverflow)
}
}

3. Exceeding the 32-Character Limit on Custom Symbols

  • Mistake: Creating a Symbol (often used as storage keys) with a string length greater than 32 characters.
  • Consequence: The Soroban VM enforces a strict 32-character limit on symbols. Calling Symbol::new(&env, "...") with a string longer than 32 characters will result in a runtime panic.
  • How to avoid/fix: Keep symbols short and descriptive. For symbols of 9 characters or less, use symbol_short! which is stored more efficiently.
  • Code Example: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// ❌ BAD: Panics at runtime (44 characters)
let key = Symbol::new(&env, "user_registration_timestamp_for_active_pool");

// ✅ GOOD: Short symbol or type-safe enum key (see intermediate section)
let key = Symbol::new(&env, "user_reg_time");
// Or:
let key = symbol_short!("reg_time");
}

4. Ignoring Result/Return Values on Safe Token Operations

  • Mistake: Calling transfer functions or contract client actions that return Result values and ignoring them via let _ = ... or not asserting success.
  • Consequence: The contract execution proceeds assuming the operation succeeded, even if it failed silently or returned an error payload, causing state inconsistency.
  • How to avoid/fix: Always handle results using Rust’s ? operator or explicitly match on them. Note that SEP-41 token operations panic on failure, but custom token logic or cross-contract invocations might return Result.
  • Code Example: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// ❌ BAD: Ignored return value could cause transaction to proceed unexpectedly
let result = token_client.try_transfer(&from, &to, &amount);
// execution continues anyway...

// ✅ GOOD: Explicitly check result and bubble up custom error
token_client.try_transfer(&from, &to, &amount)
    .map_err(|_| Error::TokenTransferFailed)?;
}

🟡 Intermediate Pitfalls

1. Unbounded Storage Growth (Gas Exhaustion)

  • Mistake: Appending items to a single shared Vec or Map under one storage key to keep track of all users or transactions.
  • Consequence: Every time the collection is read or written, the entire collection must be deserialized and serialized. As the number of users grows, the transaction CPU and memory gas usage increases linearly. Eventually, transactions will exceed the ledger limits, permanently bricking the contract and locking user funds.
  • How to avoid/fix: Store user-specific data under separate, unique keys. Use a type-safe #[contracttype] enum to represent storage key variants.
  • Code Example: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// ❌ BAD: Storing a growing list of users in a single vector under one key
pub fn register_user(env: Env, user: Address) {
    let mut users: Vec<Address> = env.storage().instance()
        .get(&symbol_short!("users"))
        .unwrap_or_else(|| Vec::new(&env));
    users.push_back(user);
    env.storage().instance().set(&symbol_short!("users"), &users);
}

// ✅ GOOD: Storing individual user flags under separate, scoped keys
#[contracttype]
pub enum DataKey {
    UserRegistered(Address),
}

pub fn register_user(env: Env, user: Address) {
    let key = DataKey::UserRegistered(user);
    env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &true);
}
}

2. State Archival Lockout (Storage Type & TTL Selection)

  • Mistake: Storing user balances in instance storage or failing to extend the Time-To-Live (TTL) of persistent storage keys.
  • Consequence:
    1. instance storage has limited size constraints. Storing user data here can cause the storage to fill up. Additionally, if the instance key expires, the contract is locked for all users and requires a costly restoration process.
    2. If persistent storage keys are not periodically extended, they will expire and be archived. Users will lose access to their data/funds until a manual, costly on-chain restoration transaction is submitted.
  • How to avoid/fix:
    1. Use instance storage only for configuration and admin addresses.
    2. Use persistent storage for user balances and user-specific structs.
    3. Regularly extend the TTL of keys when they are accessed using extend_ttl.
  • Code Example: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
pub enum DataKey {
    Balance(Address),
}

// ✅ GOOD: Access balance from persistent storage and extend its TTL
pub fn get_balance_and_bump(env: Env, user: Address) -> i128 {
    let key = DataKey::Balance(user);
    let balance: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0);
    
    // Bump TTL: if the key has less than 10,000 ledgers remaining,
    // extend its lifespan to 50,000 ledgers from the current ledger.
    env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&key, 10000, 50000);
    
    balance
}
}

3. Reentrancy and the Checks-Effects-Interactions Pattern

  • Mistake: Changing local contract state after invoking an external contract (such as a token transfer to a user).
  • Consequence: The external contract could intercept control and call back into this contract (reenter) before the local state is updated, leading to double-withdrawals.
  • How to avoid/fix: Follow the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern: perform validation checks first, write and persist local state changes next (effects), and invoke external contract calls last (interactions).
  • Code Example: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// ❌ BAD: Draining external tokens before updating internal state
pub fn claim_rewards(env: Env, user: Address) {
    user.require_auth();
    let rewards = get_pending_rewards(&env, &user);
    
    let token_client = token::Client::new(&env, &get_token_id(&env));
    token_client.transfer(&env.current_contract_address(), &user, &rewards); // Interaction
    
    // DANGER: Reentrant call could hijack control before this line executes!
    set_pending_rewards(&env, &user, 0); // Effect
}

// ✅ GOOD: State update occurs before the external transfer is initiated
pub fn claim_rewards(env: Env, user: Address) {
    user.require_auth();
    
    let rewards = get_pending_rewards(&env, &user);
    if rewards <= 0 {
        panic!("No rewards to claim"); // Check
    }
    
    set_pending_rewards(&env, &user, 0); // Effect
    
    let token_client = token::Client::new(&env, &get_token_id(&env));
    token_client.transfer(&env.current_contract_address(), &user, &rewards); // Interaction
}
}

4. Custom Signature Replay Attacks

  • Mistake: Verifying custom cryptographic signatures (e.g. Ed25519 or secp256k1) directly without binding the payload to the specific contract instance, network, and sequential transaction nonces.
  • Consequence: The signature can be intercepted by an attacker and replayed on other contracts, different networks (e.g., testnet vs. mainnet), or multiple times on the same contract to execute unauthorized actions.
  • How to avoid/fix: Use native Soroban authorization (require_auth) whenever possible, as it manages nonces and replay protection automatically. If custom verification is absolutely necessary, construct a signed payload containing:
    1. The contract’s unique address (env.current_contract_address()).
    2. The network’s passphrase ID (env.ledger().network_id()).
    3. A unique, incrementing user nonce.
  • Code Example: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// ❌ BAD: Signature payload contains only action data, vulnerable to replays
pub fn execute_custom_auth(env: Env, public_key: BytesN<32>, signature: BytesN<64>, action_data: Bytes) {
    env.crypto().ed25519_verify(&public_key, &action_data, &signature);
}

// ✅ GOOD: Signed payload binds contract address, network, and nonce
pub fn execute_custom_auth(
    env: Env, 
    user: Address, 
    public_key: BytesN<32>, 
    signature: BytesN<64>, 
    action_data: Bytes
) {
    let nonce = get_and_increment_nonce(&env, &user);
    
    let mut signed_payload = Bytes::new(&env);
    signed_payload.append(&env.current_contract_address().to_xdr_bytes());
    signed_payload.append(&env.ledger().network_id().to_xdr_bytes());
    signed_payload.append(&nonce.to_xdr_bytes());
    signed_payload.append(&action_data);
    
    env.crypto().ed25519_verify(&public_key, &signed_payload, &signature);
}
}

Documentation Style Guide

This guide defines the standards for writing and maintaining documentation in this project. Following these guidelines keeps our documentation consistent, accurate, and approachable for all readers.

Writing Standards

Tone and Voice

  • Write in a clear, direct, and friendly tone.
  • Prefer the active voice: “The compiler checks the type” rather than “The type is checked by the compiler.”
  • Address the reader as “you”. Refer to the project as “we” when describing team decisions or conventions.
  • Keep sentences short. Aim for one idea per sentence.
  • Avoid jargon unless it is defined on first use. Link to a glossary entry or explain inline.

Terminology

Use the following terms consistently throughout the documentation:

Preferred termAvoid
functionmethod (unless referring to a trait method)
cratepackage, library
commandinstruction
configurationconfig (in prose)
directoryfolder
  • Capitalize product names exactly as the project does.
  • Use code formatting for identifiers, file names, commands, and literal values (for example, Cargo.toml, cargo build).
  • Spell out acronyms on first use, for example, “Application Programming Interface (API)”.

Inclusive Language

  • Use gender-neutral language. Prefer “they” over “he/she”.
  • Avoid idioms, slang, and culture-specific references that may not translate well.
  • Use “allowlist”/“denylist” instead of “whitelist”/“blacklist”.
  • Avoid ableist terms such as “crazy”, “insane”, or “dummy” when describing code or behavior. Prefer “unexpected”, “placeholder”, or “stub”.
  • Refer to people by their roles rather than descriptors where possible.

Code Example Standards

Complete and Runnable

  • Every code example should be complete enough to compile and run unless it is explicitly marked as a fragment.
  • Include necessary imports, fn main(), and any required setup.
  • If an example is intentionally partial, indicate this with a comment such as // ... and explain what is omitted.
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let mut counts: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
    for word in ["apple", "banana", "apple"] {
        *counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }
    println!("{counts:?}");
}

no_std Compatibility

  • When an example is intended for no_std environments, state this explicitly and avoid the standard library.
  • Use #![no_std] at the crate root and document any required extern crate alloc; usage.
#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]

fn main() {
pub fn add(a: u32, b: u32) -> u32 {
    a + b
}
}

Error Handling

  • Demonstrate idiomatic error handling. Prefer Result and the ? operator over unwrap() or expect() in examples unless the example specifically illustrates panics.
  • When unwrap() is used for brevity, add a comment explaining that real code should handle the error.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::fs;

fn read_config(path: &str) -> Result<String, std::io::Error> {
    let contents = fs::read_to_string(path)?;
    Ok(contents)
}
}

Comments

  • Use comments to explain why, not what. The code itself should make the “what” clear.
  • Keep comments up to date with the code they describe.
  • Use // for inline comments and /// for documentation comments on public items.

Formatting Guidelines

Headings

  • Use sentence case for headings: “Getting started”, not “Getting Started”.
  • Do not skip heading levels. A document should start with a single # title, followed by ## sections, then ### subsections.
  • Keep headings short and descriptive.

Lists

  • Use - for unordered lists and 1. for ordered lists.
  • Keep list items parallel in structure.
  • End list items with a period only when they are complete sentences.

Code Fences

  • Always specify a language tag on fenced code blocks so syntax highlighting works correctly.
```rust
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
```
  • Use text for plain output or non-code content.
  • Keep lines within code blocks reasonably short to avoid horizontal scrolling.

Links

  • Use descriptive link text. Prefer “the configuration guide” over “click here”.
  • Use relative links for pages within the book so they work in all deployment targets.
  • Verify that links resolve before submitting changes.

Tool Recommendations

The following tools help maintain consistent, high-quality documentation:

  • mdBook — builds this documentation site. Run mdbook build in the book/ directory to verify changes compile without errors, and mdbook serve for a live preview.
  • rustfmt — formats Rust code examples consistently. Run cargo fmt before committing.
  • typos — catches spelling mistakes in prose and code. Run typos across the repository.
  • markdownlint — enforces Markdown formatting rules such as heading structure and list style. Run markdownlint 'book/src/**/*.md'.

Pre-submission Checklist

Before opening a pull request that changes documentation:

  1. Run cd book && mdbook build and confirm it succeeds without warnings.
  2. Run typos and fix any reported issues.
  3. Run markdownlint on changed files.
  4. Confirm all code examples compile and all links resolve.

Soroban Performance Benchmarks

Ducument date: The performance benchmarks for the basic examples in the Soroban Cookbook. Benchmarking is essential for understanding the gas costs and resource usage of your smart contracts on the Stellar network.

📊 Comparison Table

The following table compares the resource usage of common operations in our basic examples.

| Example | Operation | CPU Instructions (est) | RAM Usage (est) | Key Takeaway | | :— | :— | :— | :— | | 01-hello-world | hello() | ~10,000 | ~1 KB | Minimal overhead for simple logic. | | 02-storage-patterns | set_persistent | ~55,000 | ~2 KB | Persistent storage is the most expensive. | | 02-storage-patterns | set_instance | ~35,000 | ~1.5 KB | Instance storage is more efficient for config. | | 02-storage-patterns | set_temporary | ~25,000 | ~1 KB | Temporary storage is best for short-lived data. | | 02-storage-patterns | get_persistent | ~30,000 | ~1.5 KB | Reading persistent data is cheaper than writing. | | 02-storage-patterns | get_instance | ~20,000 | ~1 KB | Reading instance data is efficient for config. | | 02-storage-patterns | get_temporary | ~15,000 | ~0.8 KB | Reading temporary data is the fastest. | | 03-authentication | transfer() | ~45,000 | ~2.5 KB | require_auth() and multiple storage ops add up. | | 05-error-handling | Result return | ~12,000 | ~1.2 KB | Returning Result is cheaper than panicking. | | 11-collection-types | Vec iteration | Scales linearly | Grows with output size | Use for ordered scans and bounded butches. | | 11-collection-types | Vec mutation in storage | Scales with stored length | Grows with stored length | Good for bounded lists; avoid unbounded single-slot collections. | | 11-collection-types | Map lookup/mutation | O(log n) host ops plus storage | Higher than Vec | Use for keyed access and repeated membership checks. | | 11-collection-types | Map full iteration | Scales linearly | Grows with entry count | Sorted iteration is useful, but still costs per entry. |

Note: These values are estimates based on local test execution and may vary slightly depending on the Soroban SDK version and network configuration.

📊 Cross-Contract Call Benchmarks

Cross-contract calls introduce additional overhead compared to internal calls. The following table summarizes performance metrics for factory deployment and proxy calls, which are common patterns in composable systems.

ScenarioOperationCPU Instructions (est)RAM Usage (est)Key Takeaway
Factorydeploy contract~60,000~3 KBDeployment once per contract; reuse for multiple calls when possible.
Proxycall thrugger (cross-contract)~30,000~1.5 KBOverhead of an external call is significant; minimize the number of cross-contract calls.
Proxycall thrugger with arguments~35,000~2 KBEach additional argument increases the host function call cost.
Proxycall forward (delegate)~40,000~2.2 KBForwarding adds a small amount of overhead beyond a simple thrugger.

Note: These estimates are derived from local integration test benchmarks and may vary based on the network configuration.

⦲ Execution Time Benchmarks

While gas costs (CPU/RAM) are the primary concern for on-chain execution, local execution time is important for developer experience and integration testing.

  • Unit Tests: Most basic examples run in < 10ms per test.
  • Contract Deployment (Local): Registering a contract in the test environment takes ~5ms.
  • WASM Size: Basic contracts compile to ~10-30 KB when optimized.
  • Cross-Contract Tests: Factory deployment typically adds ~5ms per contract, while proxy calls add ~1-2 ms per call in local testing.

𝍮 Optimization Notes

Based on our benchmarks and Soroban best practices, here are several ways to optimize your contracts:

1. Storage Optimization

  • Batch Operations: Instead of calling env.storage().persistent().set() multiple times in a loop, try to consolidate data into a single Map or Vec if possible.
  • Choose the Right Type: Use Temporary storage for data that doesn’t need to persist indefinitely (e.g., nonces, temporary locks). It is significantly cheaper than Persistent storage.
  • Instance Storage for Config: Use Instance storage for shared contract configuration. It’s more efficient than Persistent for data that is frequently read but rarely changed.

2. Computational Efficiency

  • Avoid Large Loops: Gas costs scale linearly with the number of iterations. For large datasets, consider using pagination or off-chain indexing.
  • Early Exit: Validate inputs and check authorization at the very beginning of your function to avoid wasting gas on invalid requests.
  • Result over Panic: Use Result<T, E> for expected error cases. While both consume gas, structured error handling is better for contract composability and predictable behavior.

3. Collection Patterns

  • Use Vec for ordered scans: Vec append and tail removal are efficient for bounded sequences, but membership checks require O(n) scans.
  • Use Map for keyed access: Map lookup, insert, overwrite, and remove are O(log n), which is better than repeatedly scanning a Vec for keys.
  • Budget full iteration: Ved::iter(), Map::iter(), Map::keys(), and Map::values() all scale with collection size.
  • Keep stored collections bounded: Updating a collection stored as one value requires reading and writing that collection. For unbounded datasets, store entries under separate persistent keys.

4. WASM Size

  • Profile for Size: Always use opt-level = "z" in your `Cargo.toml`` release profile.
  • Minimize Dependencies: Each dependency adds to the WASM size. Use the soroban-sdk features selectively.
  • Strip Symbols: Use strip = "symbols" to remove unnecessary metadata from the binary.

5. Cross-Contract Interaction Optimization

Cross-contract calls introduce additional overhead compared to internal calls. Here are specific recommendations to minimize the perforance cost:

  • Reuse deployed contracts: If you need to call the same contract multiple times, consider deploying it once and passing its address to receiving contracts. Repeated factory deployment is costly.
  • Batch multiple calls: If you need to call several functions on the same contract, consider designing an aggregated aPI on the target contract to reduce the number of cross-contract calls.
  • Minimize data passed: Each argument increases the host function call cost. Pass only the necessary data, and prefer references or IDOs over large structures when possible.
  • Consider synchronous calls: If you need the result of a call to proceed, a synchronous call is normal. However, if you can defer or parallelize independent calls, do so to improve throughput.
  • Use throwbut and forward patterns wisely: Thruggers add overhead for each call. Forwarding adds a little more. If a contract is simply a proxy, ensure the delegation is necessary and not duplicating functionality.

🧃 How to Run Benchmarks

You can run these benchmarks yourself using the following command in each example directory:

cargo test -- --nocapture benchmark

This will run the dedicated benchmarking tests and print the resource usage (budget) to the console.

For collection benchmarks specifically:

cargo test -p collection-types benchmark -- --nocapture

For cross-contract benchmarks in the integration test suite:

cargo test -p integration-tests cross_contract_benchmark -- --nocapture

This will run the cross-contract specific benchmark tests.

📋 Benchmark Report

We ran the benchmarks described above using the Soroban test environment and the integration-tests crate. The following is a consolidated report of the storage operation benchmarks:

Read/Write Benchmarks: The table above now includes both set_* and get_* operations for each storage type. As expected, writes cost more than reads, and Persistent storage is the most expensive while Temporary is the cheapest.

Storage Type Comparison: Persistent storage is recommended only when data must survive contract upgrades. Instance storage is ideal for contract-level configuration. Temporary storage should be used for any data that does not need long-term persistence.

Iteration Benchmarks: Iterating over Vec and Map scales linearly with the number of elements. Map iteration is sorted by key and incurs similar costs to Vec iteration. For large collections, pagination is necessary to avoid exceeding the transaction budget.

Best Practices:

  • Use Temporary storage wherever possible to reduce costs.
  • Batch writes to reduce the number of storage operations.
  • Avoid unbounded single-slot collections; store large datasets under separate keys.
  • Favor Map for keyed access patterns and Vec for ordered sequences.

Full benchmark outputs can be reproduced by running cargo test -p integration-tests benchmark -- --nocapture.

Soroban & Stellar Glossary

A comprehensive glossary of terms used in Soroban smart contract development and the Stellar ecosystem.

A

Account

A Stellar account identified by a public key (G address). Accounts hold balances, can invoke contracts, and authorize operations in Soroban.

See also: Address, Identity

Address

In Soroban, an Address is a generic identifier that can represent an account, a contract, or other addressable entities. The Address type is used for authorization and identification.

Official docs: Soroban Address

Asset

A representation of value on the Stellar network. Assets can be native (XLM) or issued by accounts (custom tokens).

See also: Lumens / XLM, Token

Authorization

The process of verifying that an entity has permission to perform an action. In Soroban, this is typically done using require_auth().

See also: require_auth

B

Bytes / BytesN

Soroban SDK types for handling byte arrays. Bytes is dynamic-length, while BytesN<N> is fixed-length.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let data: Bytes = Bytes::from_slice(&env, &[1, 2, 3]);
let hash: BytesN<32> = BytesN::from_array(&env, &[0u8; 32]);
}

Bump

An operation that extends the TTL (time to live) of contract data or code in the ledger. Must be performed before data expires to keep it accessible.

See also: TTL / Time To Live, State Archival

C

Contract

A smart contract deployed on the Stellar network using Soroban. Contracts are written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly.

See also: WASM / WebAssembly, Invocation

Contract ID

A unique identifier for a deployed contract. Used to invoke contract functions and interact with the contract.

contractimpl

Rust macro that marks an implementation block as containing contract functions that can be invoked externally.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contractimpl]
impl MyContract {
    pub fn my_function(env: Env) { }
}
}

contracttype

Rust macro that marks a struct or enum as a contract type that can be stored or passed between contracts.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
pub struct MyData {
    value: u64,
}
}

Cross-contract Invocation

Calling a function in one Soroban contract from another Soroban contract. Enables composability and complex interactions between contracts on the network.

See also: Contract, Invocation

D

Deploy

The process of uploading and installing a contract on the Stellar network, making it available for invocation.

See also: Soroban CLI

E

Env

The Soroban environment object that provides access to host functions, storage, events, and other contract capabilities.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn my_function(env: Env) {
    // Access environment features
}
}

Events

Notifications emitted by contracts to log important state changes or actions. Events can be queried off-chain.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
env.events().publish((symbol_short!("transfer"),), (from, to, amount));
}

See also: Publish

Errors and Validation

The process of handling errors in Soroban contracts and validating input/state. Soroban supports custom error types with the #[derive(Debug)] macro and uses error propagation patterns similar to Rust’s Result<T, E>.

See also: Panic

F

Footprint

The set of ledger entries (storage, contracts, etc.) that a transaction will read or write. Required for resource planning.

Friendbot

A service that funds testnet accounts with test XLM for development purposes.

Testnet Friendbot: https://friendbot.stellar.org

H

Horizon

The REST API for the Stellar network. Provides access to accounts, transactions, and ledger data.

Official docs: Horizon API

Host Functions

Functions provided by the Soroban host environment that contracts can call to interact with the ledger, perform cryptographic operations, etc.

I

Identity

A key pair (public and private key) used to sign transactions and authorize operations on Stellar.

See also: Account, Soroban CLI

Instance Storage

Contract storage that persists across invocations but is specific to a contract instance. More expensive than temporary but cheaper than persistent.

See also: Persistent Storage, Temporary Storage

Invocation

The act of calling a contract function. Can be done via transactions or from other contracts.

See also: Contract

L

Ledger

The Stellar ledger is the record of all accounts, balances, and contracts on the network. Each ledger close represents a new block.

See also: Ledger Close, Ledger Entry

Ledger Close

The moment when the Stellar network validates and closes the current ledger, creating a new ledger and advancing all validators’ ledger state. Occurs approximately every 5 seconds.

Ledger Entry

A piece of data stored on the Stellar ledger, such as an account, contract code, or contract data.

Lumens / XLM

The native cryptocurrency of the Stellar network. Used for paying transaction fees and maintaining minimum account balances.

See also: Stroop

M

Mainnet

The production Stellar network where real-value transactions occur.

Network Passphrase: “Public Global Stellar Network ; September 2015”

See also: Testnet

Map

A Soroban SDK type for key-value storage. Similar to HashMap but optimized for the Soroban environment.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let mut map: Map<Address, u64> = Map::new(&env);
map.set(address, 100);
}

N

Network Passphrase

A string that uniquely identifies a Stellar network (mainnet, testnet, or custom). Required when signing transactions.

P

Panic

An unrecoverable error in Rust. In Soroban, panics cause the entire transaction to fail and revert.

See also: Errors and Validation

Persistent Storage

Contract storage that persists indefinitely (with proper TTL extension). Most expensive storage type but guarantees data persistence.

See also: Instance Storage, Temporary Storage, TTL / Time To Live

Publish

Function to emit events from a contract.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
env.events().publish((symbol_short!("event"),), (data,));
}

See also: Events

R

require_auth

A Soroban function that verifies an address has authorized the current operation. Causes transaction to fail if authorization is missing.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
user.require_auth();
}

See also: Authorization

RPC (Remote Procedure Call)

The protocol used to communicate with Soroban nodes. Required for deploying contracts and submitting transactions.

Testnet RPC: https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org

S

Soroban

The smart contract platform built on Stellar, supporting contracts written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly.

Soroban CLI

Command-line tool for building, deploying, and interacting with Soroban contracts.

soroban contract build
soroban contract deploy
soroban contract invoke

Soroban SDK

The Rust library (crate) that provides types, macros, and utilities for writing Soroban smart contracts.

Crate: soroban-sdk

State Archival

Stellar’s mechanism for managing long-term storage of contract state. Infrequently-accessed data is archived, and contracts must periodically extend the TTL of their data to keep it accessible.

Official docs: Storage and TTL

See also: TTL / Time To Live, Bump

Stellar

The blockchain network that Soroban contracts run on. Known for fast, low-cost transactions and built-in asset support.

Storage

Persistent data storage for contracts. Soroban provides three storage types: Persistent, Temporary, and Instance.

See also: Persistent Storage, Instance Storage, Temporary Storage

Stroop

The smallest unit of XLM. 1 XLM = 10,000,000 stroops.

See also: Lumens / XLM

Symbol

A Soroban type for short string identifiers, optimized for use as storage keys or event topics.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let key = symbol_short!("balance");
let long_key = Symbol::new(&env, "longer_identifier");
}

T

Temporary Storage

Contract storage that only persists for a short period (minimum 16 ledgers). Cheapest storage option, ideal for ephemeral data.

See also: Persistent Storage, Instance Storage

Testnet

A test version of the Stellar network for development. Uses test XLM with no real-world value.

Network Passphrase: “Test SDF Network ; September 2015”

See also: Mainnet, Friendbot

Token

A fungible asset on Stellar or Soroban. Can be native (XLM) or custom tokens following standards like SEP-41.

See also: Asset, Lumens / XLM, SEP-41

Transaction

A collection of operations signed by one or more accounts. In Soroban, transactions include contract invocations.

Trustline

A Stellar concept where an account explicitly trusts and can hold a specific asset issued by another account.

TTL / Time To Live

The number of ledgers that contract data will persist before expiring. Must be extended to keep data alive.

See also: Storage, Bump, State Archival

U

Unit Test

Tests that verify individual contract functions in isolation. Soroban provides test utilities for writing comprehensive tests.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[test]
fn test_my_function() {
    let env = Env::default();
    // Test code
}
}

V

Val

The base value type in Soroban. Most Soroban types can be converted to/from Val.

Vec

A Soroban SDK type for dynamic arrays. Similar to Rust’s Vec but optimized for Soroban.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let mut vec: Vec<u64> = Vec::new(&env);
vec.push_back(42);
}

W

WASM / WebAssembly

The binary format that Soroban contracts are compiled to. Provides portability and security.

Target: wasm32-unknown-unknown

See also: Contract

wasm-opt

A tool for optimizing WASM binaries to reduce size and improve performance.

wasm-opt -Oz input.wasm -o output.wasm

X

XLM

Ticker symbol for Lumens, Stellar’s native cryptocurrency.

See also: Lumens

Additional Standards

SEP-41

Stellar Ecosystem Proposal 41 - The token interface standard for Soroban, similar to ERC-20 on Ethereum.

Official spec: SEP-41

  • Soroban Examples: https://github.com/stellar/soroban-examples
  • Stellar Discord: https://discord.gg/stellardev
