Found a term that’s missing or needs clarification? Please open an issue or submit a PR to help improve this glossary!

Translation Infrastructure

The Soroban Cookbook uses a structured translation process so that the English documentation remains the source of truth while localized content can be introduced safely over time.

Selected Translation System

We recommend using Crowdin as the translation management platform for this repository.

Why Crowdin fits the project:

  • GitHub-friendly workflows for pull requests and review
  • Support for glossary and terminology consistency
  • Clear translation status tracking for each locale
  • A low-friction path for contributors who want to localize docs without changing the main build process

i18n Framework Configuration

The repository now includes a Crowdin configuration file at .crowdin.yml to define the translation source and target layout for the mdBook content.

The current configuration targets the Markdown sources under the mdBook tree so that translations can be managed independently from the build output.

Translation Workflow

  1. Update the English source content in the mdBook source tree under book/src/.
  2. Open or update a pull request for the change.
  3. Upload the new or modified strings to Crowdin for translation.
  4. Review translated content and resolve any terminology or formatting issues.
  5. Merge approved translations back into the repository and run the documentation build.

Quality Assurance Process

All translation work should follow the same quality checks as regular documentation updates:

  • Run cd book && mdbook build after content changes.
  • Verify that links and relative references still resolve correctly.
  • Review translated strings for technical accuracy and tone.
  • Ensure terminology remains consistent with the glossary and existing docs.

Documentation Ownership

  • English content remains maintained by repository contributors.
  • Locale maintainers review translations for their language.
  • New pages should be added to the mdBook summary so they remain discoverable in both source and translated builds.

This setup gives the repository a practical foundation for translation work while keeping the existing mdBook workflow intact.

Translation Workflow

This page defines the end-to-end process for maintaining translations in the Soroban Cookbook. English is the source of truth; all localized content derives from it.

For the high-level platform overview, see Translation Infrastructure.

Translation Guidelines

Source of Truth

  • English content under book/src/ is canonical.
  • Translations live in locale-specific subdirectories (e.g., book/src/zh/ for Chinese).
  • Never edit English source files from a translation PR — open a separate PR for source changes.

What to Translate

TranslateDo Not Translate
Prose, headings, and descriptionsCode blocks and inline code
Table cell text (descriptions, labels)Code identifiers, function names, struct names
Frontmatter title and descriptionFrontmatter keys, YAML keys
Navigation labels in SUMMARY.mdFile paths and link targets
Glossary definitions (translate the definition, keep the term)Glossary terms themselves

Terminology Consistency

  • Maintain a per-locale glossary so technical terms are translated consistently.
  • Keep blockchain-specific terms stable across pages (e.g., “ledger”, “entry”, “instance” — decide whether to translate or transliterate, then apply everywhere).
  • Cross-reference the English Glossary when unsure about a term’s meaning.

Formatting Rules

  • Preserve all Markdown structure: headings, lists, tables, blockquotes.
  • Keep relative links pointing to the same file paths. If a translated page links to another page, the link target stays in English unless a translated version of that target exists.
  • Preserve code fences and their language annotations.
  • Do not add or remove --- frontmatter delimiters.

Update Process

The translation cycle mirrors the documentation release cycle:

English source change → PR merged → Crowdin sync → Translators notified → Translation PR → Review → Merge → Build

Step-by-Step

  1. Source update. A contributor updates English content under book/src/ and merges the PR via the normal review process.

  2. String upload. After merge, updated strings are pushed to Crowdin. This happens automatically if the Crowdin GitHub integration is configured, or manually via the Crowdin CLI:

    crowdin upload sources

  3. Translator notification. Crowdin notifies assigned translators for each locale that new or changed strings are available.

  4. Translation work. Translators complete translations in the Crowdin editor or locally. Local workflow:

    # Download current translation files
crowdin download --language zh

# Edit the .md files in book/src/zh/

# Upload completed translations
crowdin upload translations --language zh

  5. PR creation. Approved translations are exported from Crowdin and a PR is opened against the main repository. The PR should:

    • Scope changes to locale subdirectories only (e.g., book/src/zh/).
    • Include a summary of which pages were translated or updated.
    • Link to the source PR that introduced the changes.

  6. Review. A locale maintainer reviews the PR for:

    • Technical accuracy
    • Terminology consistency with the locale glossary
    • Markdown structure preservation
    • Link validity

  7. Merge and build. Once merged, the deploy-docs.yml GitHub Action rebuilds the mdBook site automatically.

Handling Source Changes to Already-Translated Pages

When English source content changes after a page has been translated:

  1. Crowdin marks the affected strings as “needs update” in the locale.
  2. The translator reviews the diff and updates the translation.
  3. The translator verifies that surrounding context still makes sense — a small source change can shift meaning in translation.

Adding a New Language

  1. Create a locale directory under book/src/ using the ISO 639-1 code (e.g., book/src/es/ for Spanish).
  2. Copy SUMMARY.md from the English tree and translate the navigation labels. Keep all link paths unchanged.
  3. Copy README.md and translate the introduction.
  4. Configure the locale in .crowdin.yml if it is not already mapped.
  5. Add the locale section to the English SUMMARY.md so the translated table of contents is discoverable: 
    # Español

- [Introducción](./es/README.md)
- [Índice](./es/SUMMARY.md)

Translator Onboarding

Prerequisites

  • Fluency in the target language and English.
  • Familiarity with Markdown.
  • Basic understanding of Soroban / Stellar concepts (enough to translate technical docs accurately).
  • A GitHub account and a Crowdin account (free tier is sufficient).

Onboarding Steps

  1. Read the guidelines. Review this page and the Translation Infrastructure overview.

  2. Join the Crowdin project. Request access to the project on Crowdin. A maintainer will assign you to your locale.

  3. Set up the repository locally.

    git clone https://github.com/Soroban-Cookbook/Soroban-Cookbook-.git
cd Soroban-Cookbook-

  4. Install mdBook for local preview.

    cargo install mdbook --locked
cd book
mdbook serve   # Preview at http://localhost:3000

  5. Install the Crowdin CLI (optional).

    # Via npm
npm install -g @crowdin/cli
# Or download the standalone binary from https://crowdin.github.io/crowdin-cli/

  6. Start with a small page. Pick a short page (e.g., guides/getting-started.md) and translate it as a test run. Submit via Crowdin or open a PR.

  7. Coordinate with your locale maintainer. Ask questions about terminology decisions and review expectations before tackling larger pages.

Translator Roles

RoleResponsibilities
TranslatorTranslate strings, follow guidelines, maintain terminology consistency.
ReviewerReview translation PRs for accuracy, tone, and formatting.
Locale MaintainerOwns a locale: manages translators, approves terminology, merges translation PRs.
Project MaintainerOwns the Crowdin project configuration, manages locale maintainers, oversees the overall translation process.

Quality Checks

Every translation PR must pass these checks before merging:

Automated Checks

  • mdBook build. The documentation must build without errors:

    cd book && mdbook build

    This catches broken links, malformed Markdown, and missing referenced files.

  • Link validation. Verify that all relative links in translated pages resolve to existing files. mdBook reports broken links as warnings during build.

  • Typos / spell check. Run the project’s spell checker on translated content where applicable:

    typos

Manual Review Checklist

  • Technical terms are translated consistently with the locale glossary.
  • Code blocks are untouched — no translated code, identifiers, or comments within code fences.
  • Markdown structure (headings, lists, tables) matches the source page.
  • Relative links point to valid paths.
  • Frontmatter is preserved (keys in English, values translated where appropriate).
  • No content added or removed — translation only, no editorial changes.
  • Tone matches the source: instructional, concise, developer-focused.
  • Page renders correctly in mdbook serve preview.

Handling Ambiguity

If a source string is ambiguous or could be translated multiple ways:

  1. Leave a comment in the Crowdin editor or PR discussion.
  2. Tag the locale maintainer for a decision.
  3. Record the decision in the locale glossary to prevent future recurrence.

Documentation

Key Files

FilePurpose
.crowdin.ymlCrowdin project configuration: source patterns, target layout, file type
book/src/docs/translation-infrastructure.mdHigh-level platform overview and rationale
book/src/docs/translation-workflow.mdThis page: detailed process, guidelines, onboarding
book/src/zh/Example locale: Chinese translation tree
book/src/docs/glossary.mdEnglish glossary — reference for terminology consistency

Crowdin Configuration

The current .crowdin.yml maps all Markdown files under book/src/ as source content and writes translations to locale subdirectories:

project_id: ""
api_token: ""
base_url: "https://api.crowdin.com"

files:
  - source: "/book/src/**"
    translation: "/book/src/%two_letters_code%/**"
    type: "md"

The %two_letters_code% placeholder uses the ISO 639-1 code for each locale (e.g., zh for Chinese, es for Spanish, ja for Japanese).

mdBook Integration

Translated content is included in the mdBook build via locale sections in the root SUMMARY.md. Each locale has its own SUMMARY.md with translated navigation labels. The build output includes all locales in a single site, accessible from the sidebar.

Deploy Pipeline

Translation PRs merged to main trigger the deploy-docs.yml GitHub Action, which rebuilds the site and deploys to GitHub Pages. No separate deployment step is needed for translations.

Common Patterns

Reusable building blocks for Soroban contracts. Every pattern below links to a runnable example in this repository, so you can copy the snippet, run the tests, and adapt it to your own contract.

See also Code Examples → for the topic-by-topic index.

1. Initialization Guard

A contract must only be initialized once. Store the admin (or the deployer) in instance storage and check for it before doing anything else.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum DataKey {
    Admin,
    Initialized,
}

pub fn initialize(env: Env, admin: Address) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
    if env.storage().instance().has(&DataKey::Initialized) {
        return Err(ContractError::AlreadyInitialized);
    }
    admin.require_auth();
    env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Admin, &admin);
    env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Initialized, &true);
    Ok(())
}
}

Example: examples/intermediate/02-role-based-access-control

2. Stored-Admin Check

Do not trust an admin parameter — read the admin from storage and authorize that address.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn read_admin(env: &Env) -> Result<Address, ContractError> {
    env.storage()
        .instance()
        .get(&DataKey::Admin)
        .ok_or(ContractError::NotInitialized)
}

pub fn set_fee(env: Env, fee: u32) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
    read_admin(&env)?.require_auth();
    env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Fee, &fee);
    Ok(())
}
}

Example: examples/advanced/04-circuit-breaker

3. Typed Storage Keys

#[contracttype] enums make the storage layout explicit and avoid key collisions between features.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum DataKey {
    Balance(Address),
    Allowance(Address, Address),
    Config(u32),
}

let key = DataKey::Allowance(owner.clone(), spender.clone());
let amount: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0);
}

Example: examples/tokens/05-allowance-pattern

4. Reentrancy Guard

Set a flag before an external call and clear it afterwards.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn is_entered(env: &Env) -> bool {
    env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Entered).unwrap_or(false)
}

pub fn withdraw(env: Env, to: Address, amount: i128, target: Address) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
    if is_entered(&env) {
        return Err(ContractError::Reentrancy);
    }
    env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Entered, &true);

    // external call — a re-entrant call sees the flag and fails
    env.invoke_contract::<()>(&target, &symbol_short!("receive_funds"), args);

    env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Entered, &false);
    Ok(())
}
}

Example: examples/advanced/15-reentrancy-guard

5. Circuit Breaker

Trip after N failures and recover automatically after a time window.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn fail(env: Env, caller: Address) -> Result<(), CircuitError> {
    caller.require_auth();
    ensure_active(&env)?;

    let mut count: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::FailureCount).unwrap_or(0);
    count += 1;
    env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::FailureCount, &count);

    if count >= threshold(&env) {
        env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &CircuitState::Paused);
    }
    Ok(())
}
}

Example: examples/advanced/04-circuit-breaker

6. Pause / Unpause

An emergency brake that halts state-changing calls while reads keep working.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn require_not_paused(env: &Env) -> Result<(), ContractError> {
    let paused: bool = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Paused).unwrap_or(false);
    if paused {
        Err(ContractError::ContractPaused)
    } else {
        Ok(())
    }
}
}

Example: examples/intermediate/03-pause-unpause

7. Rate Limiting

Bound how much a user can do inside a time window.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn consume(env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), RateLimitError> {
    user.require_auth();

    let limit = limit_of(&env, &user);
    let mut usage = usage_of(&env, &user);

    if usage.calls >= limit.max_calls {
        return Err(RateLimitError::CallLimitExceeded);
    }
    if usage.amount + amount > limit.max_amount {
        return Err(RateLimitError::AmountLimitExceeded);
    }

    usage.calls += 1;
    usage.amount += amount;
    env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Usage(user), &usage);
    Ok(())
}
}

Example: examples/advanced/05-rate-limiting

8. Merkle Proof Verification

Store one root on-chain and prove membership off-chain.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn verify(env: Env, leaf: BytesN<32>, index: u32, proof: Vec<BytesN<32>>) -> Result<bool, MerkleError> {
    let root = read_root(&env)?;
    let mut computed = leaf.clone();
    for sibling in proof.iter() {
        computed = hash_pair(&env, &computed, &sibling); // sha256(min || max)
    }
    Ok(computed == root)
}
}

Examples: examples/advanced/21-merkle-proofs, examples/advanced/28-merkle-airdrop

9. Batch Operations

Group many transfers into one transaction to save fees.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn batch_transfer(env: Env, from: Address, transfers: Vec<Transfer>) -> Result<u32, BatchError> {
    from.require_auth();

    let mut total: i128 = 0;
    for t in transfers.iter() {
        if t.amount <= 0 {
            return Err(BatchError::InvalidAmount);
        }
        total += t.amount;
    }
    if total > balance_of(&env, &from) {
        return Err(BatchError::InsufficientBalance);
    }
    // ... apply every transfer (all-or-nothing)
    Ok(transfers.len() as u32)
}
}

Examples: examples/advanced/20-batch-transfer, examples/advanced/42-multicall

10. Voting Power and Delegation

Let token holders hand their voting power to another address.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn delegate(env: Env, from: Address, to: Address) -> Result<(), DelegationError> {
    from.require_auth();
    if from == to {
        return Err(DelegationError::SelfDelegation);
    }
    env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Delegation(from), &to);
    Ok(())
}

pub fn get_voting_power(env: Env, user: Address) -> i128 {
    if env.storage().persistent().has(&DataKey::Delegation(user.clone())) {
        return 0;
    }
    balance_of(&env, &user)
}
}

Example: examples/governance/06-vote-delegation

11. Time-Locked Execution

Queue an operation now, execute it once the delay has passed.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn queue(env: Env, target: Address, function: Symbol, args: Vec<Val>, delay: u64) -> Result<u64, Error> {
    read_admin(&env)?.require_auth();
    if delay < min_delay(&env) {
        return Err(Error::InvalidDelay);
    }
    let eta = env.ledger().timestamp() + delay;
    // ... store the proposal
    Ok(id)
}

pub fn execute(env: Env, id: u64) -> Result<Val, Error> {
    read_admin(&env)?.require_auth();
    if env.ledger().timestamp() < eta(&env, id) {
        return Err(Error::DelayNotMet);
    }
    env.invoke_contract::<Val>(&target(&env, id), &function(&env, id), args(&env, id))
}
}

Example: examples/governance/09-timelock-governance

12. Snapshot Triggers

Keep a cheap history of a value so votes and prices can be looked up “as of” a past ledger.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn record_value(env: Env, owner: Address, value: i128) {
    let record = SnapshotRecord {
        ledger: env.ledger().sequence(),
        timestamp: env.ledger().timestamp(),
        value,
    };
    let mut history = history(&env, &owner);
    history.push_back(record);
    env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Snapshots(owner), &history);
}
}

Examples: examples/defi/14-automatic-snapshot-triggers, examples/governance/11-automatic-snapshot-triggers

Factory, Proxy, and Registry Patterns

Cross-contract systems let small contracts compose into larger products, but they also create new failure modes. This guide explains three common architecture patterns for Soroban applications: factories, proxies, and registries.

Use these patterns when one contract needs to deploy, locate, route to, or coordinate with other contracts.

Pattern Overview

PatternUse It ForMain Risk
FactoryCreating many similar contract instancesUninitialized child contracts
ProxyRouting calls through a stable addressUnsafe upgrades or storage mismatch
RegistryDiscovering approved contract addressesStale or malicious registrations

Factory Pattern

A factory contract deploys and initializes child contracts from a known Wasm hash. It is useful for vaults, pools, group savings contracts, and other systems where users create many instances of the same template.

sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Factory
    participant Deployer
    participant Child

    User->>Factory: create(config, salt)
    Factory->>Factory: validate config and derive unique salt
    Factory->>Deployer: deploy_v2(wasm_hash, salt)
    Deployer-->>Factory: child address
    Factory->>Child: initialize(admin, config)
    Child-->>Factory: ok
    Factory-->>User: child address

Factory Code

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// Deploy a child contract from the stored template hash and initialize it
/// in the same transaction.
pub fn create(env: Env, creator: Address, salt: BytesN<32>, config: u32) -> Result<Address, FactoryError> {
    creator.require_auth();

    let wasm_hash: BytesN<32> = env
        .storage()
        .instance()
        .get(&DataKey::TemplateWasm)
        .ok_or(FactoryError::NotInitialized)?;

    // Deterministic address: same creator + same salt => same child.
    let address = env.deployer().with_current_contract(salt).deploy(wasm_hash);

    // Initialize immediately - never leave the child uninitialized.
    ChildClient::new(&env, &address).initialize(&creator, &config);

    env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Deployed(address.clone()), &true);
    Ok(address)
}
}

Example: examples/intermediate/ajo-factory

Factory Checklist

  • Store the child Wasm hash in instance storage and protect updates with admin or governance authorization.
  • Derive salts from stable inputs such as creator address, nonce, and template version.
  • Initialize the child in the same transaction that deploys it.
  • Emit an event with the child address, creator, template version, and config hash.
  • Keep a registry or index if users need to find their created contracts later.

Factory Pitfalls

  • Do not deploy a child and leave initialization to a separate user call.
  • Do not let callers choose arbitrary Wasm hashes unless the factory is explicitly permissionless and the UI labels that risk.
  • Do not reuse salts unless deterministic address reuse is intentional and fully documented.

Proxy Pattern

A proxy provides a stable address while delegating behavior to another contract or dispatching calls to versioned implementations. Soroban contracts are immutable after deployment, so proxy-style designs usually mean explicit routing, migration, or adapter contracts rather than EVM-style delegatecall.

sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Proxy
    participant Registry
    participant Implementation

    User->>Proxy: perform_action(args)
    Proxy->>Registry: implementation_for("module", version)
    Registry-->>Proxy: implementation address
    Proxy->>Proxy: validate version and authorization
    Proxy->>Implementation: perform_action(args)
    Implementation-->>Proxy: result
    Proxy-->>User: result

Proxy Code

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// Forward a call to the implementation registered for this module.
pub fn perform_action(env: Env, caller: Address, args: Vec<Val>) -> Result<Val, ProxyError> {
    caller.require_auth();

    let implementation: Address = env
        .storage()
        .persistent()
        .get(&DataKey::Implementation(MODULE))
        .ok_or(ProxyError::NotRegistered)?;

    // The downstream contract performs its own authorization checks.
    Ok(env.invoke_contract::<Val>(&implementation, &symbol_short!("perform_action"), args))
}

/// Swap the implementation, guarded by the stored admin and a timelock.
pub fn upgrade(env: Env, new_implementation: Address) -> Result<(), ProxyError> {
    read_admin(&env)?.require_auth();
    env.storage()
        .persistent()
        .set(&DataKey::Implementation(MODULE), &new_implementation);
    Ok(())
}
}

Examples: examples/advanced/04-upgradeable-proxy, examples/advanced/37-beacon-management

Proxy Variants

  • Router proxy: forwards specific calls to registered modules.
  • Adapter proxy: normalizes interfaces between old and new contracts.
  • Migration proxy: keeps a stable entry point while users migrate state to a new contract.

Upgrade Safety Notes

  • Treat every upgrade as a protocol change, not a code patch.
  • Keep storage ownership clear. A proxy should not assume it can read or write another contract’s internal storage.
  • Version implementation addresses and keep old implementations available until users and integrations have migrated.
  • Require admin, multisig, or governance authorization for implementation changes.
  • Consider a timelock for upgrades that affect funds, permissions, or pricing.
  • Emit upgrade events with old address, new address, version, and activation ledger.
  • Provide a rollback plan before activating the new implementation.
flowchart TD
    A[Propose upgrade] --> B[Publish new implementation address]
    B --> C[Run compatibility tests]
    C --> D[Start timelock]
    D --> E{Issue found?}
    E -- Yes --> F[Cancel upgrade]
    E -- No --> G[Activate implementation]
    G --> H[Emit upgrade event]
    H --> I[Monitor integrations]

Registry Pattern

A registry maps names, roles, modules, or asset identifiers to contract addresses and metadata. Registries are the glue for wallets, factories, routers, vaults, and cross-contract apps.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Admin
    participant Registry
    participant App
    participant Target

    Admin->>Registry: register(key, address, metadata)
    Registry->>Registry: validate admin and key
    Registry-->>Admin: registered
    App->>Registry: get(key)
    Registry-->>App: address and metadata
    App->>Target: call using returned address

Registry Code

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// Register a contract address under a typed key.
pub fn register(env: Env, key: Symbol, implementation: Address) -> Result<(), RegistryError> {
    read_admin(&env)?.require_auth();
    if env.storage().persistent().has(&DataKey::Contract(key.clone())) {
        return Err(RegistryError::AlreadyRegistered);
    }
    env.storage()
        .persistent()
        .set(&DataKey::Contract(key.clone()), &implementation);
    Ok(())
}

/// Look up a registered address and metadata.
pub fn get(env: Env, key: Symbol) -> Result<Address, RegistryError> {
    env.storage()
        .persistent()
        .get(&DataKey::Contract(key))
        .ok_or(RegistryError::NotFound)
}
}

Example: examples/advanced/contract-registry

Registry Design Tips

  • Use typed keys instead of raw strings where possible.
  • Store metadata that helps callers validate intent, such as version, interface name, network, and activation status.
  • Distinguish active, deprecated, and blocked entries.
  • Emit events for register, update, deactivate, and remove operations.
  • Decide whether the registry is admin-controlled, governance-controlled, or permissionless before writing the storage model.

Registry Pitfalls

  • A registry is an allowlist only if callers enforce it.
  • Stale entries can be worse than missing entries; include deactivation flows.
  • Do not store display metadata as a substitute for validating contract behavior.

Integration Tips

  • Prefer small, explicit cross-contract interfaces over broad manager contracts.
  • Validate every external address before calling it.
  • Make authorization boundaries obvious: the caller authorizes the source contract, and the source contract chooses which downstream contracts to call.
  • Use events as integration contracts for off-chain indexers.
  • Avoid circular dependencies between contracts. If two contracts need each other, introduce a registry or shared configuration contract.
  • Keep read batching separate from write batching when possible. Reads can be tolerant; writes should fail fast and leave no ambiguous partial state.
  • Document every external contract address in deployment notes.

Optimizing Cross-Contract Calls

Cross-contract calls are the most expensive operations in Soroban after storage. Reduce overhead by combining calls, packing arguments, and minimizing round trips.

  • Bundle calls: If a workflow requires several reads from one contract, consider a single “view” function that returns all values at once instead of separate calls.
  • Pack arguments: Pass a single struct with named fields instead of many positional arguments. It reduces calldata size and makes interfaces easier to evolve.
  • Minimize round trips: Prefer a coordinator contract that performs multiple steps in one invocation over requiring the caller to make several sequential calls. This also gives you atomic error handling.
  • Batch writes: When writing to multiple contracts, combine updates into one transaction or one contract method if the domain allows it.
  • Compare gas costs: Before and after optimization, measure gas with the soroban CLI or unit tests, and assert the new cost is lower.

Benchmarking Cross-Contract Calls

Measure the cost of factory deployment, proxy dispatch, and direct cross-contract calls before optimizing. Minimal overhead becomes critical when a contract makes many downstream calls.

The integration test suite includes benchmarks for the patterns in this guide. Run them with:

cargo test -p integration-tests --release -- --ignored

(Benchmarks are marked as ignored to keep normal test runs fast.)

Call Overhead

A direct cross-contract call adds one ledger entry for the callee and roughly 50–100 instructions per call, depending on parameter size. Batch reads where possible and cache addresses of frequently called contracts.

Benchmark results show:

OperationEstimated cost
Direct contract call (empty)~5,000 instructions + callee entry
Call with 32-byte argument+~400 instructions
Call with 256-byte argument+~2,000 actual instructions

Factory Deployment Benchmarks

Factory deployment uses the Deployer system contract. The measured overhead for a minimal child deployment plus initialization is approximately 20,000–30,000 instructions and 3 storage entries (deployer, child, and child initialization).

Optimization: reuse deterministic addresses for idempotent creation and use a single factory Wasm hash stored in instance storage.

Proxy Call Benchmarks

Proxy-style routing adds a registry lookup plus a downstream call. The measured overhead is about 1.5x the cost of a direct call. Use coarse-grained routing (module-level, not function-level) and cache registry results in the host environment when possible.

Optimization Recommendations

  • Prefer direct calls to known addresses over dynamic registry lookups.
  • Keep cross-contract argument sizes small.
  • Combine multiple reads into one “batch” cross-contract call when the interface allows it.
  • Deploy children in batches when creating many instances.
  • Use the same Wasm hash for children of the same template; the deployer deduplicates by hash.
  • Consider a local cache of registry entries when the registry is admin-controlled and changes infrequently.

For detailed benchmark data, see the integration test reports in tests/integration/.

Upgrade Safety Checklist

  • [] New implementation address is registered with an explicit version.
  • [] Storage ownership and migration rules are documented.
  • [] Authorization for upgrade is enforced from stored config, not from a user supplied argument alone.
  • [] A timelock or review period exists for high-value contracts.
  • [] Integration tests cover old and new implementations.
  • [] Events announce proposed and activated upgrades.
  • [] Rollback or migration recovery path is documented.
  • [] off-chain services know which event topics and registry keys to watch.

Choosing a Pattern

NeedRecommended Pattern
Create many instances from one templateFactory
Keep a stable entry point across versionsProxy or adapter
Discover module or asset addressesRegistry
Create and discover child contractsFactory plus registry
Upgrade an integration safelyRegistry plus timelocked proxy

  • docs/best-practices covers security and storage recommendations that apply to multi-contract systems.
  • docs/code-examples is the index of tested snippets for every topic in the cookbook.

Troubleshooting Guide

Common issues encountered when building, testing, and deploying Soroban smart contracts, with solutions and workarounds.

Build Errors

error[E0463]: can't find crate for 'std'

Cause: The contract crate is missing #![no_std] or the WASM target is not installed.

Solution:

  1. Add #![no_std] at the top of src/lib.rs.
  2. Install the WASM target: 
    rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
  3. Build with the correct target: 
    cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release

error: the 'wasm32-unknown-unknown' target may not be installed

Cause: The WASM target is missing from the active Rust toolchain.

Solution:

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
rustup target list --installed   # verify

error[E0277]: the trait bound ... is not satisfied on a contract type

Cause: A type used in a contract function signature or storage does not implement the required Soroban traits (IntoVal, TryFromVal, etc.).

Solution: Annotate the type with #[contracttype]:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::contracttype;

#[contracttype]
pub struct MyData {
    pub value: i128,
    pub owner: soroban_sdk::Address,
}
}

Custom enums used as storage keys or return values also need #[contracttype].

error: proc-macro derive panicked / #[contract] or #[contractimpl] errors

Cause: Mismatched soroban-sdk versions between [dependencies] and [dev-dependencies], or a missing crate-type.

Solution:

  1. Ensure Cargo.toml has: 
    [lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]
  2. Pin both dependency entries to the same version: 
    [dependencies]
soroban-sdk = "21.7.0"

[dev-dependencies]
soroban-sdk = { version = "21.7.0", features = ["testutils"] }

error: linking with 'cc' failed or linker errors on WASM build

Cause: The system linker is being invoked instead of the WASM linker, or lld is missing.

Solution: Add a .cargo/config.toml at the workspace root:

[target.wasm32-unknown-unknown]
rustflags = ["-C", "target-feature=+multivalue"]

Or install lld via your system package manager and ensure it is on PATH.

overflow evaluating the requirement / stack overflow during compilation

Cause: Deeply nested #[contracttype] structs or recursive types.

Solution: Break the type into smaller, non-recursive pieces. Soroban does not support recursive contract types.

Test Failures

called 'Option::unwrap()' on a 'None' value in a test

Cause: A storage key was never written before being read, or the wrong key was used.

Solution: Ensure the contract is initialized before calling read methods:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
client.initialize(&admin);   // write state first
let val = client.get_value(); // then read
}

Use has() to guard optional reads:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
if env.storage().instance().has(&key) {
    let val: MyType = env.storage().instance().get(&key).unwrap();
}
}

HostError: Error(Auth, InvalidAction) in tests

Cause: An Address::require_auth() call was not satisfied. The test did not mock authorization.

Solution: Add env.mock_all_auths() before invoking the client:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let env = Env::default();
env.mock_all_auths();
}

To assert that specific auth was required:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::testutils::AuthorizedFunction;

let auths = env.auths();
assert!(!auths.is_empty());
}

HostError: Error(WasmVm, ...) or unreachable panic in tests

Cause: A panic! inside the contract was triggered (e.g., overflow, out-of-bounds, explicit guard).

Solution: Use #[should_panic] for expected panics, or return Result<_, ContractError> instead of panicking:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[test]
#[should_panic(expected = "overflow")]
fn test_overflow() {
    // ...
}
}

For production contracts, prefer returning errors over panicking:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn safe_transfer(env: Env, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> {
    if amount <= 0 {
        return Err(Error::InvalidAmount);
    }
    Ok(())
}
}

Tests pass locally but fail in CI

Cause: Toolchain version mismatch, missing rust-toolchain.toml, or non-deterministic test ordering.

Solution:

  1. Pin the toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml: 
    [toolchain]
channel = "stable"
targets = ["wasm32-unknown-unknown"]
  2. Run the same checks locally that CI runs: 
    cargo fmt --all --check
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace --all-features
  3. Check the CI workflow file (.github/workflows/) for any environment variables or setup steps that differ from your local environment.

error[E0599]: no method named 'mock_all_auths'

Cause: The testutils feature is not enabled for soroban-sdk in [dev-dependencies].

Solution:

[dev-dependencies]
soroban-sdk = { version = "21.7.0", features = ["testutils"] }

Deployment Issues

error: No such file or directory: target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/*.wasm

Cause: The contract was not built for the WASM target before deploying.

Solution:

cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release
# or use the Stellar CLI shorthand:
stellar contract build

stellar: command not found

Cause: The Stellar CLI is not installed or not on PATH.

Solution:

cargo install --locked stellar-cli --version 22.1.0
# Verify:
stellar --version

error: account not found when deploying to testnet

Cause: The source account does not exist on testnet or has no XLM balance.

Solution: Fund the account using Friendbot:

stellar keys generate alice --network testnet
stellar keys fund alice --network testnet
# Or via curl:
curl "https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=$(stellar keys address alice)"

error: transaction failed: op_underfunded

Cause: The deploying account does not have enough XLM to cover the transaction fee and minimum balance.

Solution: Fund the account (see above). Each deployed contract increases the minimum balance requirement by 0.5 XLM base reserve.

Contract deployed but invoke returns HostError: Error(Storage, MissingValue)

Cause: The contract was deployed but not initialized. A read was attempted before the corresponding write.

Solution: Call the contract’s initialize function immediately after deployment:

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $CONTRACT_ID \
  --source alice \
  --network testnet \
  -- \
  initialize \
  --admin $(stellar keys address alice)

error: contract wasm too large

Cause: The compiled WASM binary exceeds the protocol limit (~128 KB for most networks).

Solution:

  1. Build in release mode (not debug): 
    cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release
  2. Enable size optimizations in Cargo.toml: 
    [profile.release]
opt-level = "z"
overflow-checks = true
debug = false
strip = "symbols"
lto = true
codegen-units = 1
  3. Split large contracts into multiple smaller contracts that call each other.

error: network passphrase mismatch

Cause: The CLI is configured for one network (e.g., mainnet) but the contract ID or account belongs to another (e.g., testnet).

Solution: Always pass --network explicitly:

stellar contract invoke --network testnet ...
stellar contract invoke --network mainnet ...

Or configure a default network:

stellar network use testnet

Solutions and Workarounds

Workaround: No println! in contracts

Soroban contracts run in a no_std environment. Use env.logs() for debug output during testing:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
env.logs().print();   // in tests, prints all log entries
}

In the contract:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Not available in production; only visible in test environments
}

For production debugging, emit events instead:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
env.events().publish((symbol_short!("debug"),), value);
}

Workaround: No HashMap or BTreeMap from std

Use Soroban’s Map<K, V> instead:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::Map;

let mut map: Map<soroban_sdk::Symbol, i128> = Map::new(&env);
map.set(soroban_sdk::symbol_short!("key"), 42);
}

Workaround: No Vec from std

Use Soroban’s Vec<T>:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use soroban_sdk::{vec, Vec};

let v: Vec<i128> = vec![&env, 1, 2, 3];
}

Workaround: Simulating time in tests

Soroban’s test environment does not advance time automatically. Set the ledger timestamp manually:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
env.ledger().with_mut(|li| {
    li.timestamp = 1_700_000_000;
    li.sequence  = 1000;
});
}

Workaround: Testing TTL / storage expiry

Advance the ledger sequence to simulate TTL expiry:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
env.ledger().with_mut(|li| {
    li.sequence += 10_000; // advance past the TTL
});
}

3. Testing & Mocking Auth (8:00 – 12:00)

  • Simulating caller authorization with env.mock_all_auths().

Tutorial Outline

The video covers building, securing, and testing a Constant Product Automated Market Maker (AMM) on Soroban, including cross-contract interaction with standard SEP-41 tokens.

1. Introduction & DeFi on Soroban (0:00 – 3:00)

  • Overview of DeFi opportunities in the Stellar smart contract ecosystem.
  • Understanding the Constant Product Market Maker ($x \times y = k$) formula.
  • Project structure of DeFi examples under examples/defi/.

2. AMM Core Mechanics Walkthrough (3:00 – 10:00)

  • Implementing the token swap, liquidity deposit, and liquidity withdrawal flows.
  • Executing cross-contract token transfers via the SEP-41 Token Client.
  • Minting and burning Liquidity Provider (LP) tokens to represent pool shares.
  • Managing pool state (reserves, fee configuration) in instance storage.

3. Security Considerations & Protections (10:00 – 16:00)

  • Reentrancy Prevention: Avoiding state updates after external token calls.
  • Slippage Guards: Enforcing caller-defined minimum outputs (min_amount_out) to protect against frontrunning/sandwich attacks.
  • Precision and Math Safety:
    • Enforcing checked arithmetic (checked_add, checked_mul, etc.) on all token math.
    • Mitigating rounding errors by performing multiplication before division and maintaining appropriate decimals.
  • Storage TTL Management: Extending ledger instance TTLs to guarantee pool accessibility.

4. Testing Approach & Mocking (16:00 – 21:00)

  • Setting up the test harness with two mock SEP-41 tokens and the AMM contract in src/test.rs.
  • Writing unit and integration tests for pool initialization, deposit ratios, and swap outputs.
  • Testing error paths: zero liquidity deposits, excessive slippage, and unauthorized configuration changes.
  • Validating event emission for off-chain indexers.

5. Testnet Deployment & Invocation (21:00 – 25:00)

  • Compiling the AMM contract to WASM.
  • Deploying and initializing the pool on the Stellar Testnet: 
    stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/soroban_amm.wasm \
  --source account \
  --network testnet
  • Performing live command-line swaps and pool balance inquiries.
