Architecture Decision Records

This section contains Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for the Soroban Cookbook project.

ADRs document significant architectural and design decisions — the context that led to them, the decision itself, and the consequences. They live in version control alongside the code so the reasoning is never lost.

What is an ADR?

An ADR is a short document that captures a single architectural decision. Each ADR describes:

  • Context — the situation and constraints that made a decision necessary
  • Decision — what was decided and why
  • Consequences — what becomes easier, harder, or different as a result

ADRs are immutable once accepted. If a decision changes, a new ADR is written to supersede the old one. This preserves the full history of how the project evolved.

Index

ADRTitleStatus
ADR-001Record Architecture DecisionsAccepted
<<<<<<< HEAD
ADR-002Rust VersionAccepted
ADR-003Soroban SDK VersionAccepted
ADR-004Testing FrameworkAccepted
ADR-005Documentation PlatformAccepted
=======
ADR-002Select Storage Tier by LifetimeProposed
ADR-003Keep Storage Keys Stable and Manage TTL ExplicitlyProposed
ADR-004Authenticate Before Protected State ChangesProposed
ADR-005Use Least-Privilege Access ControlProposed
ADR-006Guard Contract Code UpgradesProposed
ADR-007Version and Migrate Persistent State ExplicitlyProposed

8c99210 (Create Pattern Selection ADRs) | ADR-008 | Use mdBook for Documentation | Accepted | | ADR-009 | Workspace Structure and CI Exclusion Mechanism | Accepted | | ADR-010 | Soroban SDK Version Migration Strategy | Accepted | | ADR-011 | Code Coverage Toolchain (tarpaulin + Codecov) | Accepted | | ADR-012 | Example Naming Convention (Numeric Prefixes) | Accepted |

Creating a New ADR

  1. Copy template.md to a new file named NNN-short-title.md (e.g. 002-workspace-structure.md)
  2. Fill in all sections — context, decision, and consequences
  3. Set the status to Proposed
  4. Open a PR; once merged and agreed upon, update the status to Accepted
  5. Add the new ADR to the index table above and in docs/adr/README.md

ADR Statuses

StatusMeaning
ProposedUnder discussion, not yet decided
AcceptedDecision made and in effect
DeprecatedNo longer relevant but kept for history
Superseded by ADR-NNNReplaced by a newer decision

Further Reading

  • Michael Nygard’s original ADR article
  • ADR GitHub organization

1. Record Architecture Decisions

Date: 2026-02-19

Status

Status: Accepted

Context

As the Soroban Cookbook grows, we need a way to document important architectural and design decisions. These decisions affect the structure, patterns, and approaches used throughout the project. Without documentation, the reasoning behind decisions is lost over time, making it difficult for new contributors to understand why things are the way they are.

We need a lightweight, accessible method to:

  • Record the context and reasoning behind significant decisions
  • Track the evolution of the project’s architecture
  • Help new contributors understand the project’s design philosophy
  • Provide a reference for future decisions
  • Document trade-offs and their consequences

Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) are a proven approach used by many open-source projects to solve this problem. They provide a simple, text-based format that lives in version control alongside the code.

Decision

We will use Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to document significant architectural and design decisions in the Soroban Cookbook project.

Implementation details:

  • ADRs will be stored in docs/adr/ directory
  • Each ADR will be a markdown file named NNN-title-with-dashes.md
  • ADRs will use the template defined in docs/adr/template.md
  • ADRs are numbered sequentially (001, 002, 003, etc.)
  • ADRs are immutable once accepted (we create new ADRs to supersede old ones)
  • This first ADR documents the decision to use ADRs

What qualifies as an ADR:

  • Choice of project structure or organization
  • Selection of major dependencies or frameworks
  • Significant design patterns or approaches
  • Testing strategies and quality standards
  • Security or performance-critical decisions
  • Build, deployment, or CI/CD approaches

What does NOT need an ADR:

  • Minor implementation details
  • Bug fixes
  • Documentation updates
  • Routine maintenance
  • Example-specific decisions (document in example README instead)

Consequences

Positive

  • Transparency: Contributors can understand why decisions were made
  • Onboarding: New contributors can quickly learn the project’s philosophy
  • Accountability: Decisions are documented and can be reviewed
  • Learning: The project’s evolution is visible and traceable
  • Reduced bike-shedding: Past decisions are documented, reducing repeated debates
  • Historical context: We preserve the reasoning even when team members change

Negative

  • Additional overhead: Takes time to write ADRs for decisions
  • Maintenance: Need to keep ADRs organized and up to date
  • Learning curve: Contributors need to learn the ADR process
  • Potential for outdated info: Old ADRs may no longer reflect current reality

Neutral

  • Discipline required: Team must commit to writing ADRs consistently
  • Not everything needs an ADR: Judgment required on what qualifies
  • Living with decisions: ADRs make it explicit when we’re stuck with past choices

References

  • Michael Nygard’s original ADR article
  • ADR GitHub organization
  • GitHub’s ADRs

Notes

Future ADRs to consider:

  • Project structure (workspace organization)
  • Testing approach and coverage standards
  • CI/CD pipeline design
  • Documentation site architecture
  • Example organization and categorization
  • Versioning and release strategy

This ADR itself serves as an example of the format and level of detail expected in future ADRs.

2. Rust Version

Date: 2026-10-19

Status

Status: Accepted

Context

The Soroban Cookbook workspace compiles a large set of smart-contract examples and tests against the Soroban SDK. Rust versions affect:

  • WASM output compatibility with the Soroban host
  • Available language features in example code
  • Compiler diagnostics and Clippy lint availability
  • Reproducibility of CI builds across contributor machines

We need a single, pinned Rust version so that:

  • Every contributor produces the same build artefacts
  • CI is deterministic and not affected by nightly regressions
  • The WASM target (wasm32-unknown-unknown) is always present

Several constraints apply:

  • The Soroban SDK specifies a minimum supported Rust version (MSRV) of 1.74 as of SDK 29.x
  • Some example patterns require const generics and let-chains that need ≥ 1.74
  • The project wants a recent stable compiler but not nightly (which is unstable)
  • All contributors must be able to reproduce builds by running rustup show

Decision

Pin Rust to 1.96.0 (stable) using a rust-toolchain.toml at the workspace root:

[toolchain]
channel = "1.96.0"
targets = ["wasm32-unknown-unknown"]
components = ["rust-src"]

Why 1.96.0:

  • Well above the SDK’s MSRV of 1.74
  • Latest stable release tested against Soroban SDK 29.x at the time of this ADR
  • Ships with improved const-evaluation and Clippy lints used in the codebase
  • Supported by all major CI runners (ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest)

What is pinned:

  • Compiler version: 1.96.0
  • Target: wasm32-unknown-unknown (required for Soroban contract compilation)
  • Component: rust-src (required for -Z build-std in WASM profiles)

Update policy:

  • Pin is updated when the Soroban SDK releases a new MSRV requirement or when a new stable fixes a reproducibility or security issue
  • Updates are tracked as new ADRs that supersede this one
  • Dependabot monitors rust-toolchain.toml via the rust ecosystem entry in .github/dependabot.yml

Consequences

Positive

  • Fully reproducible builds across all contributors and CI environments
  • rustup automatically installs the correct toolchain when contributors clone the repo
  • No “it works on my machine” issues caused by compiler version drift
  • Clippy and rustfmt versions are also pinned, keeping style checks consistent

Negative

  • Contributors must update their toolchain when the pin is bumped
  • We occasionally miss language features available in newer stable releases until the pin is updated
  • A pinned old toolchain may mask future deprecation warnings earlier than necessary

Neutral

  • The rust-toolchain.toml override is respected by Cargo, rust-analyzer, and most editors without any extra configuration
  • Nightly features are out of scope; if a future example requires them, a separate ADR must justify the change

References

  • rust-toolchain.toml specification
  • Soroban SDK 29.x changelog
  • Current pin: rust-toolchain.toml

Notes

Verify compatibility after each SDK major version upgrade by running:

rustup update 1.96.0
cargo test --workspace
cargo build --workspace --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release

3. Soroban SDK Version

Date: 2026-10-19

Status

Status: Accepted

Context

Every smart-contract example in the Soroban Cookbook depends on the soroban-sdk crate. The SDK:

  • Defines the core types (Env, Address, Map, Vec, …) used in every contract
  • Determines which host functions are available and their signatures
  • Has a release cadence tied to the Stellar Protocol upgrade schedule
  • Can introduce breaking API changes between major versions

We need a workspace-level SDK version policy so that:

  • All examples compile against the same SDK
  • Contributors are not surprised by version mismatches
  • Security patches and protocol changes are adopted quickly

Two broad approaches were considered:

  1. Per-crate pinning — each example Cargo.toml specifies its own version range
  2. Workspace-level pinning — a single [workspace.dependencies] entry is the source of truth

Decision

Pin soroban-sdk at 29.0.0 as a workspace dependency:

# Cargo.toml (workspace root)
[workspace.dependencies]
soroban-sdk = "29.0.0"

Each example crate inherits the version with:

# examples/<category>/<name>/Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
soroban-sdk = { workspace = true }

Why 29.0.0:

  • Production-stable release aligned with Stellar Protocol 21
  • Includes the soroban_sdk::token interface required by the DeFi and token examples
  • SEP-41 token interface is stable in this version
  • Compatible with Rust 1.96.0 (see ADR-002)

Update policy:

  • The workspace pin is bumped in a dedicated PR that also updates all example code for breaking API changes
  • RC versions (-rc.N) may be used in a next branch to test upcoming SDK changes before they land in main
  • Major version bumps require a new ADR superseding this one
  • Minor/patch bumps update this ADR’s version table in-place (no new ADR required)

Version history:

SDK VersionDate AdoptedNotes
29.0.02026-10-19Initial ADR; production stable, Protocol 21

Consequences

Positive

  • One place to update when the SDK changes; all examples stay in sync automatically
  • CI catches any example that fails to compile after an SDK bump
  • Contributors never need to hunt for the “correct” SDK version for a new example

Negative

  • All examples must be updated simultaneously on a major version bump — a larger but bounded one-time cost
  • RC releases in the workspace affect every example, so they are kept to the next branch
  • Examples temporarily broken by an SDK breaking change block merges until fixed

Neutral

  • The soroban-sdk crate bundles soroban-env-host as an internal dependency; host version mismatches are therefore invisible to example authors
  • Workspace inheritance does not prevent individual crates from overriding the version if truly needed (they should document the reason)

References

  • soroban-sdk crates.io page
  • soroban-sdk GitHub releases
  • Current workspace pin: Cargo.toml

Notes

When bumping the SDK version:

  1. Update [workspace.dependencies] in the root Cargo.toml
  2. Run cargo test --workspace and fix any compilation errors
  3. Run cargo build --workspace --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release
  4. Update the version history table in this ADR
  5. Open a PR titled chore: bump soroban-sdk to X.Y.Z

4. Testing Framework

Date: 2026-10-19

Status

Status: Accepted

Context

The Soroban Cookbook contains Rust smart-contract examples that run on the Soroban VM. Testing smart contracts presents unique requirements compared with ordinary Rust programs:

  • Contracts execute inside a sandboxed host environment; unit tests must simulate that environment
  • Cross-contract calls require orchestrating multiple contract instances within a single test
  • Gas and resource accounting must be verifiable
  • Security-focused tests (reentrancy, authorization bypass) need a dedicated home
  • Fuzz testing is useful for serialization and arithmetic boundaries

The project evaluated three testing layers:

  1. Native Rust unit tests — fast, in-process, no harness required
  2. Soroban test utilities (soroban_sdk::testutils) — in-process Soroban environment simulation
  3. Standalone integration harness — separate workspace member with shared fixtures

We also evaluated external tools:

  • cargo-nextest — parallel test runner; drop-in replacement for cargo test
  • cargo-tarpaulin — coverage measurement for CI
  • cargo-fuzz — libFuzzer-based fuzz testing

Decision

Use a four-layer testing strategy implemented entirely with standard Cargo tooling:

Layer 1 — Example unit tests (src/test.rs)

Every example crate includes in-module tests using the soroban_sdk::testutils environment:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use soroban_sdk::testutils::Address as _;
    use soroban_sdk::Env;
    // ...
}
}

These tests cover the happy path and basic error cases for a single contract.

Layer 2 — Integration tests (tests/integration/)

A dedicated workspace member (tests/integration) holds cross-contract and multi-step workflow tests. It has path dependencies on the example crates it orchestrates, ensuring the tests always build against the current source.

Layer 3 — Security tests (tests/security/)

A separate workspace member isolates authorization-bypass, reentrancy, and access-control regressions. Keeping them separate prevents them from inflating example-level test counts and makes threat-model coverage easy to audit.

Layer 4 — Fuzz targets (tests/fuzz/)

cargo-fuzz targets cover serialization and arithmetic boundaries. These run in CI on a schedule (not on every PR) due to their long execution time.

Tooling decisions

ToolDecisionReason
cargo testDefault test runnerNo extra installation, works everywhere
soroban_sdk::testutilsIn-process host simulationOfficial SDK-provided harness, no external process needed
cargo-tarpaulinCoverage measurementWorks with wasm32 exclusions, uploads to Codecov
cargo-fuzzFuzz testinglibFuzzer-backed; standard Rust fuzz tool

cargo-nextest is not adopted as a required tool because it adds a non-trivial installation step. Contributors may use it locally, but CI relies on cargo test.

Coverage target

Maintain ≥ 90% line coverage across all example crates, measured by cargo-tarpaulin in CI.

Consequences

Positive

  • Zero additional build-tool installation required beyond a standard Rust toolchain
  • Tests run identically on Windows, macOS, and Linux (cross-platform CI)
  • Separation of concerns: unit, integration, security, and fuzz tests do not interfere
  • Coverage gate in CI prevents regressions from reaching main
  • soroban_sdk::testutils provides a deterministic, reproducible host environment

Negative

  • Tests do not run against a live Soroban network; on-chain edge cases require manual testing
  • The four-crate layout adds navigation overhead for new contributors (mitigated by README files in each directory)
  • cargo-tarpaulin does not support WASM targets; WASM tests are excluded from coverage counts

Neutral

  • cargo-nextest can be used locally to speed up test runs without affecting CI parity
  • Fuzz targets accumulate coverage corpora over time; those corpora are .gitignore-d to keep repo size bounded

References

  • soroban-sdk testutils documentation
  • cargo-tarpaulin
  • cargo-fuzz
  • Integration test README: tests/integration/README.md
  • Security test README: tests/security/README.md

Notes

When adding a new example:

  1. Add unit tests in src/test.rs for single-contract behavior
  2. If the example interacts with other contracts, add a test in tests/integration/
  3. If the example handles authorization or untrusted input, add a case in tests/security/
  4. Run cargo tarpaulin --package <crate-name> locally to verify coverage before opening a PR

5. Documentation Platform

Date: 2026-10-19

Status

Status: Accepted

Context

The Soroban Cookbook needs a documentation platform that:

  • Builds from the markdown files already authored alongside the code
  • Deploys automatically to GitHub Pages via CI (.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml)
  • Allows contributors to preview changes locally with a single command
  • Supports a structured sidebar (SUMMARY.md) matching the repository layout
  • Keeps the authoring barrier low for Rust-focused contributors who are not JavaScript developers

Two platforms were evaluated in detail (see Documentation Platform Evaluation):

mdBook — a static site generator written in Rust, designed for book-style documentation

Docusaurus — a React-based static site generator with richer UI customization

Additional platforms considered but quickly eliminated:

  • MkDocs — Python-based; adds a second language toolchain with no benefit over mdBook for this use case
  • GitBook — cloud-hosted; raises vendor lock-in concerns and costs money at scale
  • Astro — requires significant front-end work; overkill for reference-heavy content

Decision

Use mdBook as the primary documentation platform, deployed from the book/ directory.

book/
  book.toml         # mdBook configuration
  src/
    SUMMARY.md      # sidebar / table of contents
    *.md            # documentation pages
    adr/            # Architecture Decision Records
    docs/           # reference material
    guides/         # step-by-step guides
    examples/       # example write-ups

Build command:

cd book && mdbook build

Local preview:

cd book && mdbook serve

Why mdBook over Docusaurus:

FactormdBookDocusaurus
Build tool languageRust (fits the project)JavaScript (extra toolchain)
Contributor overheadMinimalModerate–high
Local build speedExcellentModerate
Existing repo alignment✅ Already adopted❌ Would require migration
Migration costNoneHigh
Interactive UI / search tuningLimitedGood
Marketing / landing pagesWeakStrong

The project does not currently need marketing pages, versioned docs, or custom search facets — the three main Docusaurus advantages. Those needs are served by the webapp/ surface.

Scope split by platform:

SurfacePlatformPurpose
book/mdBookTechnical docs, guides, examples, ADRs
docs/Markdown (no build)Supporting reference notes, operational docs
webapp/Custom ReactInteractive playground, community showcase

Migration trigger criteria (if two or more become true, revisit this ADR):

  1. Versioned documentation becomes a hard requirement
  2. The docs homepage must serve as the primary public marketing site
  3. Custom search facets are required inside the docs site
  4. Contributor demand shifts strongly toward UI-rich discovery

Consequences

Positive

  • Zero new toolchain dependencies: mdBook is already installed in CI
  • SUMMARY.md provides an explicit, reviewable table of contents that new contributors can read
  • Fast local previews (mdbook serve) encourage documentation contributions
  • Pages are pure markdown, making diffs readable and reviews straightforward
  • The existing deploy-docs.yml workflow continues without changes

Negative

  • Limited built-in search (mdBook’s default search is basic)
  • UI customization requires Handlebars templates and custom CSS rather than React components
  • Community-facing discovery features (filtering, cards) must live in webapp/ rather than the docs site

Neutral

  • Docusaurus remains a future option; the structured SUMMARY.md and markdown-first approach make a future migration straightforward if the trigger criteria are met
  • The docs/ directory continues to hold supporting reference material without a build step; only book/ is published

References

  • mdBook documentation
  • mdBook GitHub
  • Documentation Platform Evaluation
  • Current build workflow: .github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml
  • Current configuration: book/book.toml

Notes

To add a new page to the documentation:

  1. Create a markdown file in the appropriate book/src/ subdirectory
  2. Add an entry to book/src/SUMMARY.md
  3. Run cd book && mdbook build to verify no broken links
  4. Open a PR — the deploy workflow publishes changes automatically on merge to main

2. Select Storage Tier by Lifetime

Date: 2026-10-21

Status

Status: Proposed

Context

Soroban offers persistent, instance, and temporary storage with different lifetime, TTL, and rent behavior. A single default tier either increases cost or risks data expiring sooner than the application expects.

Decision

Choose the tier from the data’s required lifetime and access pattern:

  • Use temporary storage only for short-lived, reconstructable data; account for its expiration.
  • Use instance storage for small, contract-wide configuration and state whose lifetime follows the contract instance.
  • Use persistent storage for durable, independently keyed application state; manage each entry’s TTL explicitly.

Do not describe persistent data as permanent: every tier has lifecycle and archival constraints that the contract must handle.

Consequences

Positive

  • Storage cost and expiration behavior match the purpose of each value.
  • TTL renewal and recovery requirements are visible during design.

Negative

  • Code must select a tier deliberately and handle expiry where applicable.
  • Moving data between tiers later may require a migration.

Neutral

  • The storage tier is an application-level choice, not a substitute for access control or backups.

References

  • Soroban storage guidance: https://developers.stellar.org/docs/smart-contracts/data/storage-types
  • Example: examples/basics/02-storage-patterns/

Notes

Review tier choices when retention requirements or protocol limits change.

3. Keep Storage Keys Stable and Manage TTL Explicitly

Date: 2026-10-21

Status

Status: Proposed

Context

Storage keys are part of a contract’s persistent data schema. Ad hoc keys and unplanned TTL renewal make collisions, accidental data loss, and future upgrades harder to reason about.

Decision

Represent keys with a typed #[contracttype] enum or struct, including the address or identifier that scopes each record. Treat serialized key shapes as stable: do not repurpose a key for a different value or silently change its encoding. Introduce a new key/schema and an explicit migration when the shape must change.

For persistent and instance entries, set TTL renewal thresholds and target lifetimes intentionally. Renew before the entry reaches its archival boundary; test both normal access and expiry/recovery behavior. Temporary entries must remain safe to lose when their TTL expires.

Consequences

Positive

  • Key ownership and data shape are easier to audit and test.
  • Schema changes become explicit upgrade work instead of accidental breakage.

Negative

  • Typed keys and migration paths add some implementation overhead.
  • TTL policy needs maintenance as protocol limits and retention needs evolve.

Neutral

  • Existing key formats remain usable; this decision governs new and changed storage schemas.

References

  • Soroban storage guidance: https://developers.stellar.org/docs/smart-contracts/data/storage-types
  • Example: examples/basics/02-storage-patterns/
  • Related: ADR-002

Notes

Include storage key compatibility and TTL renewal in upgrade reviews.

4. Authenticate Before Protected State Changes

Date: 2026-10-21

Status

Status: Proposed

Context

Contract entry points often receive an address identifying the actor or owner of an asset. Checking application permissions alone does not prove that the address authorized the invocation, and omitting that check can expose state to unauthorized changes.

Decision

Call Address::require_auth() for the address that must authorize an action before performing protected state mutations. Then apply separate business authorization checks, such as ownership, role membership, allowance, or state-transition rules. A caller-supplied address is not proof of permission by itself.

For delegated actions, record the grant explicitly and authenticate the delegate when it exercises that grant. Keep authorization scope limited to the operation and data the grant is intended to cover.

Consequences

Positive

  • Authentication and application-level authorization remain distinct and auditable.
  • Unauthorized state changes fail before contract state is modified.

Negative

  • Clients must provide the required authorization entries.
  • Each entry point must identify whose authorization is required.

Neutral

  • Read-only operations may remain public when the data and application policy permit it.

References

  • Soroban authorization: https://developers.stellar.org/docs/learn/fundamentals/authorization
  • Example: examples/basics/03-authentication/

Notes

Test missing authorization, wrong actor, and delegated authorization paths.

5. Use Least-Privilege Access Control

Date: 2026-10-21

Status

Status: Proposed

Context

Some contracts need only one administrator; others have distinct capabilities such as minting, pausing, and configuration. A single broad admin role is simple but grants more authority than many operations require. Fine-grained roles add state and administration complexity.

Decision

Use the simplest model that represents the actual trust boundaries:

  • Use a stored owner/admin for a small contract with one coherent privileged capability.
  • Use named, least-privilege roles when capabilities are independently granted, revoked, or exercised.
  • Authenticate the actor and check the stored owner or role membership on each privileged entry point. Protect role grants and revocations with an explicit role-administration policy.
  • Use multisig or governance authority for high-impact administration where operational risk warrants it; add a timelock for changes that need a review window.

Do not infer a role hierarchy from enum ordering or naming; encode the permitted capabilities explicitly.

Consequences

Positive

  • Routine operators receive only the permissions they need.
  • Privileged actions and role changes have clear authorization boundaries.

Negative

  • Role-based systems require careful grant, revoke, and recovery procedures.
  • Multisig and timelocks add operational latency and integration work.

Neutral

  • Permissionless entry points remain valid when their behavior is safe for any caller.

References

  • Soroban authorization: https://developers.stellar.org/docs/learn/fundamentals/authorization
  • Examples: examples/basics/03-authentication/, examples/advanced/03-rbac-modifiers/
  • Related: ADR-004

Notes

Review administrator recovery and key rotation alongside role design.

6. Guard Contract Code Upgrades

Date: 2026-10-21

Status

Status: Proposed

Context

Soroban contract code is not replaced merely by deploying a new Wasm artifact. An in-place update requires an explicit contract upgrade path; systems without that path need a new contract or explicit routing architecture. An unsafe upgrade can change critical behavior without giving users time to review it.

Decision

When a contract supports in-place Wasm replacement, require authenticated governance or admin approval and use a proposal workflow with a review delay, cancellation path, and events for proposal and activation. Verify and record the Wasm hash before activation. Use a multisig or governance address for production authority when appropriate.

If a contract has no safe in-place upgrade path, deploy a versioned replacement or an explicit router/adapter and document how clients move to it. Do not assume EVM-style delegatecall or automatic sharing of storage between contracts.

Consequences

Positive

  • Upgrade authority, code identity, and review windows are explicit.
  • Users and integrators can observe proposed and activated changes.

Negative

  • Timelocks can delay urgent fixes; emergency procedures need separate review.
  • New-contract routing requires compatibility and client migration work.

Neutral

  • A pause mechanism can limit incident impact but does not replace a safe upgrade process.

References

  • Example: examples/advanced/03-proxy-admin/
  • Example: examples/advanced/04-upgradeable-proxy/
  • Soroban upgrade guidance: https://developers.stellar.org/docs/smart-contracts/contract-upgrades

Notes

Test authorization, cancellation, delay enforcement, replay prevention, and the exact Wasm hash activated.

7. Version and Migrate Persistent State Explicitly

Date: 2026-10-21

Status

Status: Proposed

Context

Replacing contract code does not transform existing storage values. A change to key encoding, value shape, or state ownership can therefore make old state unreadable or leave it stranded. Large migrations may also exceed transaction resource limits if performed in one call.

Decision

Treat persistent storage as a versioned schema. Preserve compatibility for existing keys where practical; otherwise add an explicit migration with a version marker, authorization, and observable progress. Make migration steps idempotent and bounded so they can safely resume across transactions. Define which version each entry uses and how normal entry points behave while migration is incomplete.

When moving to a different contract address, do not assume the new contract can read the old contract’s storage. Specify and test an explicit export/import, user-driven migration, or routing plan before deployment.

Consequences

Positive

  • Upgrades have a defined compatibility and recovery path.
  • Bounded, repeatable work is easier to test against transaction limits.

Negative

  • Migration logic increases code size and requires fixtures from prior versions.
  • Some migrations require user participation or multiple transactions.

Neutral

  • A migration may be unnecessary when a code update preserves the existing storage schema; record that compatibility check in the upgrade review.

References

  • Example: examples/advanced/04-upgradeable-proxy/
  • Example: examples/advanced/03-proxy-admin/
  • Related: ADR-003, ADR-006

Notes

Test migration from representative old-state fixtures, including repeated execution and partial completion.

8. Use mdBook for Documentation

Date: 2026-11-20

Status

Status: Accepted

Context

The cookbook needs a documentation site that renders the markdown written next to the examples, deploys to GitHub Pages from CI, and can be previewed locally with one command. Most contributors are Rust developers, so a JavaScript toolchain would raise the barrier to editing docs.

Alternatives considered (see the Documentation Platform Evaluation):

  • Docusaurus — React-based and highly customizable, but requires Node.js and React knowledge to maintain
  • MkDocs — Python-based; adds a second language toolchain with no clear benefit
  • GitBook — hosted service; vendor lock-in and cost at scale

Decision

Use mdBook as the documentation platform. The book lives in book/, its sidebar is book/src/SUMMARY.md, and it is deployed by .github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml.

  • Build: cd book && mdbook build
  • Preview: cd book && mdbook serve

mdBook was chosen over Docusaurus because it is a single Rust binary that fits the project’s existing toolchain, uses plain markdown with no MDX or React, and is the same tool used for the Rust Book, which most learners already know.

Consequences

Positive

  • One toolchain (Rust/Cargo) for code and docs
  • Contributors edit plain markdown; no front-end build knowledge needed
  • Fast local builds and simple CI deployment

Negative

  • Less UI customization than Docusaurus (no React components, limited theming)
  • Features such as versioned docs or rich search need preprocessors or custom JS

Neutral

  • Every new page must be added to SUMMARY.md to appear in the sidebar

References

  • Book ADR-005: Documentation Platform
  • mdBook documentation

Notes

Revisit this decision if the project needs versioned documentation or interactive components that mdBook cannot support.

9. Workspace Structure and CI Exclusion Mechanism

Date: 2026-11-20

Status

Status: Accepted

Context

The cookbook holds many independent example contracts. They need to build and test together so that SDK upgrades and shared code changes are verified everywhere, but a few crates cannot always build with the rest:

  • Learner templates (templates/dao-governance-dapp, templates/token-dapp) are standalone Cargo workspaces meant to be copied out, and a package cannot belong to two workspaces
  • During an SDK migration, some examples may temporarily fail to compile
  • Host-only crates (integration tests, fuzz harness) cannot be built for wasm32v1-none

Alternatives considered:

  • Independent crates, no workspace — every example pins its own dependencies; SDK versions drift and CI must loop over crates
  • One workspace with every crate always required — a single broken example blocks all CI

Decision

Use a single root Cargo workspace (Cargo.toml) that lists each example under members and pins shared dependencies such as soroban-sdk in [workspace.dependencies].

  • Standalone template workspaces are listed under exclude in the root Cargo.toml, with a comment explaining why
  • CI runs cargo through scripts/ci-workspace.sh, which reads scripts/ci-exclude-packages.txt and passes --exclude <pkg> for each entry; crates that are temporarily broken go in that file and are removed once fixed
  • The same exclude list is applied to the tarpaulin coverage job
  • ci-workspace.sh build also excludes host-only crates (integration-tests, security-tests, soroban-cookbook-fuzz) for the wasm build

Consequences

Positive

  • One cargo test --workspace verifies every example against the same SDK
  • A broken crate can be parked without blocking unrelated PRs
  • Exclusions are explicit, version-controlled and reviewable

Negative

  • New examples must be added to members or they are silently not built
  • Excluded crates can rot if entries are not removed after they are fixed

Neutral

  • Templates are built by their own CI workflow (templates.yml), outside the root workspace

References

  • Root Cargo.toml (members / exclude)
  • scripts/ci-workspace.sh and scripts/ci-exclude-packages.txt
  • .github/workflows/test.yml

Notes

Keep scripts/ci-exclude-packages.txt free of package entries except while a migration or fix is in progress.

10. Soroban SDK Version Migration Strategy

Date: 2026-11-20

Status

Status: Accepted

Context

All examples depend on soroban-sdk, which ships breaking changes across major versions in step with Stellar protocol upgrades. The cookbook moved from SDK 26 to the 28 release candidate (28.0.0-rc.1) and then to 29.0.0. During these moves some examples stopped compiling, and the templates and fuzz harness drifted from the workspace version.

Alternatives considered:

  • Per-example upgrades over time — each example bumps its own SDK; the repo ends up with mixed versions and inconsistent teaching material
  • Big-bang upgrade with no fallback — CI stays blocked until every example is fixed

Decision

Upgrade the SDK at the workspace level, in one place, with a temporary exclusion list as a safety valve:

  1. Dependabot (or a maintainer) bumps soroban-sdk in [workspace.dependencies]; every example inherits it via soroban-sdk = { workspace = true }
  2. Examples that no longer compile are fixed in the same PR where practical; otherwise they are added to scripts/ci-exclude-packages.txt (see ADR-009) and fixed in follow-up PRs
  3. Standalone templates and the fuzz harness are bumped to the same version so they stay in sync with the workspace
  4. Release candidates may be adopted to get ahead of protocol changes, then replaced by the stable release
  5. Stale version references in comments and docs are updated once the migration is complete

Consequences

Positive

  • All examples teach a single SDK version
  • CI immediately shows which examples a new SDK breaks
  • Migrations can land incrementally without blocking unrelated work

Negative

  • A major bump touches many crates at once and needs coordinated review
  • Excluded crates are untested until they are fixed

Neutral

  • The current workspace version and its history are tracked in Book ADR-003: Soroban SDK Version

References

  • Root Cargo.toml ([workspace.dependencies])
  • scripts/ci-exclude-packages.txt
  • Soroban SDK releases

Notes

A migration is complete when scripts/ci-exclude-packages.txt has no package entries left.

11. Code Coverage Toolchain (tarpaulin + Codecov)

Date: 2026-11-20

Status

Status: Accepted

Context

The cookbook is teaching material, so example tests should exercise the code they demonstrate. The project needs coverage that runs in CI, works for a Cargo workspace, gives reviewers feedback on PRs, and is easy to reproduce locally.

Alternatives considered:

  • cargo-llvm-cov — accurate source-based coverage, but needs the llvm-tools component and extra setup
  • grcov — flexible, but requires instrumented builds and more configuration
  • Coveralls — hosted service similar to Codecov, with weaker patch-coverage reporting

Decision

Use cargo-tarpaulin to measure coverage and Codecov to report it.

  • tarpaulin.toml configures workspace-wide coverage, writes Cobertura XML, HTML and LCOV reports to coverage/, and sets fail-under = 90
  • The coverage job in .github/workflows/test.yml installs (and caches) tarpaulin, applies the CI exclude list, and uploads the XML report with codecov/codecov-action
  • codecov.yml keeps project coverage informational and requires 90% patch coverage on changed lines
  • Contributors run cargo tarpaulin locally with the same configuration

Consequences

Positive

  • Single command for local and CI coverage
  • PR comments and patch targets make untested new code visible
  • Historical trends and badges via Codecov

Negative

  • tarpaulin only runs on Linux x86_64, so macOS/Windows contributors need CI or a container
  • Line coverage is less precise than LLVM source-based coverage
  • Coverage builds are slower than normal test runs

Neutral

  • Test modules, build artifacts and docs are excluded from coverage metrics

References

  • tarpaulin.toml
  • codecov.yml
  • .github/workflows/test.yml (coverage job)
  • cargo-tarpaulin

Notes

Switching to cargo-llvm-cov would only change the CI job and local command; the Codecov setup could stay the same.

12. Example Naming Convention (Numeric Prefixes)

Date: 2026-11-20

Status

Status: Accepted

Context

Examples are grouped by category (basics, intermediate, advanced, defi, tokens, nfts, governance, storage). Learners need a clear order to follow within each category, and maintainers need directory names that sort predictably in file browsers, the book sidebar and the workspace members list.

Alternatives considered:

  • Plain descriptive names (hello-world, custom-errors) — no implied learning order; listings sort alphabetically
  • Separate ordering file — order is defined outside the directory itself and easily drifts

Decision

Name example directories examples/<category>/NN-short-name, where NN is a two-digit number giving the suggested reading order within the category, and short-name is lowercase kebab-case (for example examples/basics/01-hello-world, examples/tokens/01-sep41-token).

  • Numbers are scoped to a category, not global
  • New examples take the next free number in their category
  • Closely related variants may share a number (for example 13-collection-types and 13-queue-variants)
  • Book pages for examples mirror the directory name (for example book/src/examples/tokens/01-sep41-token.md)

Consequences

Positive

  • Directory listings sort in learning order
  • The number gives learners an obvious next step
  • Book pages and example directories map one-to-one

Negative

  • Inserting an example in the middle of a sequence means reusing a number or renumbering
  • A few older directories without a prefix (for example examples/hello-world, examples/basics/lazy-cache) do not follow the convention

Neutral

  • Crate names in Cargo.toml are independent of the numeric prefix

References

  • examples/README.md
  • book/src/SUMMARY.md

Notes

Renaming existing directories to fill gaps is not required; prefer stable paths over a perfectly contiguous sequence.
